Oftentimes the credentials will stay active for a certain period of time. Only until you click log out will it terminate the session, right? And the same with the computer. If we log into the computer and then we get up and go to the break room or something, does that terminate our session? No, it doesn't. So that means an attacker could possibly hijack that session, and that's what we're trying to prevent. So the way that we do that, first of all, is we implement what's called session timeouts. So timeouts will close a session after a set period of time of inactivity. So if I log in and then I go to the break room to get a drink or whatever, right? And I take more than five minutes, if I configure the system to say, if I am inactive for five minutes, then terminate the session. That means when I come back, I will have to re-authenticate to the system to restart that session. So effectively, the inactivity closed the session for me. Now, you can set it between 5 minutes, 15 minutes. It really depends on your organization and also the industry standard, right? What is the industry regulation? What are the industry standards? Whether it's PCI or HIPAA or FISMA or whatever it is, right? You have to know those, and that's what you would end up setting as part of your configuration. And this would be set on your network devices, your computers, your mobile devices, and so on, right? Any endpoint or computer that can accept a timeout, you would want to do this. And also you want to consider doing this as a network configuration as well. So any communication sessions traversing over the router or switch or firewall, they will terminate after a certain period of inactivity as well. And the timeout will effectively require authentication so that you can resume the system activity again after that timeout has been invoked, right? So once the timeout has been activated, the session is terminated, now you need to identify and authenticate again in order to start a new session. And that is the timeout, the goal behind these. And a really effective way to implement this is using screensavers. Now, this is predominantly used on Windows, but it can be implemented on Linux and Unix just the same, as well as macOS as well. The screensaver is designed to protect the information that's on the screen itself. So let's say you got an important phone call. You're working on a really sensitive document, you get a phone call, something's on fire in the computer room, and you got to run over and check on it, right? And you forgot to lock your screen, or you forgot to sign out, and you just left everything up on your screen, right? Well, now that sensitive data is available for anybody to walk by and read. The screensaver will activate after a time of inactivity. So we can set it for five minutes, we can set it for 10 minutes, 15 minutes, whatever the policy in your organization has determined that it will activate. Effectively what will happen is an image will pop up, or an animated screen will pop up, you know, boxes moving around or something really cool in the background kind of thing, and it will protect the contents that are on the screen. Then you can require authentication in order to reestablish the session after the screensaver time limit expires. So if it's activated after five minutes, in order to remove the screensaver, you're going to have to enter your authentication credentials to get access to the session again, okay? And then your session timeout would timeout based on whatever it's set to. So let's say, for instance, I set my screensaver to five minutes and my session timeout as 10 minutes. So the screensaver would activate in five minutes. Then if I don't re-authenticate to the screensaver, then my session's going to timeout, right? Then I have to log in all over again, okay? So that's the idea behind those. And what we're trying to protect against are the session attacks that come along with this, specifically session hijacking or also called sidejacking. This is when an attacker will target unsecure session tokens or cookies or open a wireless network, okay? Session hijacking is a type of man-in-the-middle attack. So this is where an attacker is between you and the endpoint that you're communicating with. And they're either sniffing or eavesdropping on the network connection, or they're eavesdropping on the wireless network connection, and they're watching how you're interacting, right? And they're trying to capture your session credentials, and that's what we're talking about here. There's also a session fixation, which is when an attacker plants an unsecure session token or cookie on your browser, right? On a victim's browser. And that's so they can use your token to accomplish what's called a replay attack. So now that the attacker has your token and credential, they will use that to replay your session while giving you a fake token so that you cannot re-authenticate to your session, okay? And that helps them gain unauthorized access. So just to give you an idea how this looks, you have users who are authenticated to a website, right? They signed in, gave their password. I don't know why they're using my username, but anyway. So now you get a token from that website, right? A cookie or a token of some kind. Well, if you have your man in the middle who's watching this transaction, maybe they capture that token as part of sniffing, and then what they do is they take that token, they use that token, and they create a fake token, and then they place that on your machine. Then use your valid token to replay your session on this website and gain unauthorized access to your account, right? Pretty scary stuff. And that's exactly what we're trying to prevent. So how do we defend against this? Well, obviously we want to encrypt session traffic if and at all possible, right? If we can do it, we want to do that so we can protect the session communications and prevent that sniffing or eavesdropping on the wire or on the wireless, right? We also want to configure components to close user sessions after a set period of time. So we want to configure those timeouts, right? Whether it's direct console, remote access, web access, they should all have session timeouts configured. And again, that's typically between 5 to 15 minutes of inactivity, right? And then we also want to include logout features wherever possible on any of our applications. We want to make it visible and easy for our users to access. So they can click sign out or logout, or end session, or whatever you want to call it. But we want them to manually close their active session because when they click that, so long as it's configured properly, it will terminate their credentials, it'll invalidate the tokens, it'll invalidate their certificates or whatever it is, okay? And that's what we want to do there. Also, we want to enforce account lockouts so that way if someone is trying to replay credentials, that we can lock that account out. And this prevents against a brute force attack where an attacker is trying different credentials in order to guess a password or guess an account name, trying to get access to the account. And if we set this to three login attempts or five login attempts, if they fail at the third login attempt, then it will lock the account and they can no longer access the system with that account. Same with five or however many you want to set it to. And then we want to limit simultaneous sessions from the same user. This is also called concurrent sessions as well. You don't want a user having 10 sessions open to the same application. So this can set you up for a denial of service attack, a distributed denial of service attack, and also it can permit replay attacks as well. Normally, you'll lock these down to between one to three sessions, depending on the system and depending on the industry standards and regulations. But this will prevent an attacker from using your credentials to replay or play back your session. So the bottom line for session management, understand the different ways to manage sessions, know the session attacks we talked about, and also know the session management security considerations.```

Here’s a **structural summary** of the video on *Session Management* for the CISSP exam:

---

## 1. Definition of a Session
- A connection and exchange between two entities (e.g., user–computer, computer–application).
- Uses protocols like TCP or UDP.
- Sessions have **IDs** that bind a user’s credentials to the active session.

---

## 2. Session Management Scope
- **Initiation**, **management**, and **proper termination** of sessions.
- Risk: closing a browser or stepping away does **not** always terminate a session → possible **session hijacking**.

---

## 3. Key Security Control: Session Timeouts
- Closes a session after a set period of **inactivity**.
- Requires **re-authentication** to resume.
- Typical timeout: **5–15 minutes** (depends on org policy or industry regs like PCI, HIPAA, FISMA).
- Applied to:
  - Endpoints (computers, mobile devices)
  - Network devices (routers, switches, firewalls)

---

## 4. Screensavers as a Session Protection Tool
- Activates after inactivity (e.g., 5 min).
- Hides on-screen sensitive data.
- Requires **authentication to dismiss** and resume session.
- Can be combined with longer session timeout (e.g., screensaver at 5 min, session timeout at 10 min).

---

## 5. Session Attacks

| Attack | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Session hijacking (sidejacking)** | Attacker steals session token/cookie (e.g., over unsecured wireless) → man-in-the-middle attack. |
| **Session fixation** | Attacker plants an unsecure token on victim’s browser → later uses it for a **replay attack**. |

---

## 6. Defenses Against Session Attacks

1. **Encrypt session traffic** (prevent sniffing/eavesdropping).
2. **Configure timeouts** for all access types (console, remote, web).
3. **Include logout features** – visible and easy to use → invalidates tokens/credentials.
4. **Enforce account lockouts** (e.g., after 3–5 failed attempts) → blocks brute force.
5. **Limit simultaneous/concurrent sessions** (typically 1–3) → prevents replay and DoS/DDoS.

---

## 7. Bottom Line for CISSP
- Know **how to manage sessions** (initiation, active control, termination).
- Recognize **session attacks** (hijacking, fixation, replay).
- Apply **security considerations** (timeouts, encryption, lockouts, concurrency limits).

```Welcome to this video on Password Attacks. In the previous video, we talked about single and multi-factor authentication, and part of single-factor authentication is using a password. So in this video, we're going to focus on the different attacks that are likely to occur against passwords. And if you recall from the previous video, a password is just the credential that is used to authenticate an identity. Our identity being our username, the password being the secret credential that we know that proves that we are who we claim to be. Now, passwords are nothing more than just secret character codes often used to authenticate a subject. It's a passphrase, it's a combination of characters, it's whatever we want it to be, it can also be a pin number, it could be a lot of different things. But it's secret meaning we only know it, unless somebody discovers it, and that's the bad part. And that's exactly what this video is all about. There are also cognitive passwords as well. These are answers to questions that were created during the registration process for your authentication credentials. And an example of this is, where did you meet your spouse, what is your favorite food or drink, what is your pet's name, where were you born, you know, those kinds of things. These are also called security questions. Now, these are typically done with self-service password systems, that way users can reset their passwords on their own by answering these questions with their cognitive passwords. Now, some attacks that you might see on the exam, really every password attack is going to start with a brute-force attack. This is an attempt to guess a password by using every possible combination of characters. You're trying everything, you're trying every combination of everything. Now, there's a lot of different attacks that fall under the category of brute-force, and we'll talk about those here. But this is just mainly the high level category of the type of attack, brute force attack, where you're guessing. It's also called a password guessing attack as well. Then there's a dictionary attack. These use common words or a dictionary file in attempt to guess your password. So the dictionary file could be created by an attacker with known passwords that maybe they got from the internet, from the dark web, maybe they bought something and there's a a bunch of passwords in this file. Maybe they're just known common words that are used for passwords. Maybe they're from decrypted passwords that were recovered at some point. There's a lot of different ways to go about this. Tools like hashcat, John the ripper, certain tools like that can compare hashes and derive hashes and attempt to come up with passwords. Then once we have a collection of those passwords, we can put them in a file and then install them into the tool, and then the tool can inject these into different login forms and so on. So dictionary attack uses common words or a dictionary file in order to attempt to guess a password. So this is a type or form of a brute-force attack. There's also what's called a spraying attack. This uses a single password across multiple login accounts to gain unauthorized access. So you're using the same password, but you're using multiple different login names. So the attacker will create a password like CISSP123. And then they're going to use that same password across all the different applications they think it might work. What we're trying to avoid here is getting locked out of the account. So we're going to try different login names, different user names, whatever it is, and we're going to use the same password over and over and over. Now, there are automated tools that will do this for us, this isn't a manual exercise. But this helps us to avoid locking out the account, that way we can try different passwords at a later time. There's also credential stuffing, which is the automated use of stolen credentials to gain unauthorized access. So again, this is an automated way to inject the names, the usernames and passwords into login forms. And this can come from stolen credentials, this can come from discover credentials from say, some other attacks and things like that. Both of these are forms of brute-force attacks as well. And before we move on, let me show you an example of how some of these work. And this is an example from OWASP.org. So let's say we compromise a website database here, and this becomes our file, this becomes our password file, and we have SpongeBob, and we have Sally and krabs, and we have Patrick, we have admin, we have all these usernames, with all of the passwords as well. So again, in credential stuffing, what you see here, the attacker is just going to try all these combinations against these login forms. Every possible combination against all these different login forms. Whereas in a password spraying attack, we're just going to use this one password. Then we're going to use that same password with SpongeBob. We're going to use that same password with Squidward. We're going to use that same password with Sally and so on and so on and so on. And tools, again, will help us do this. Now again, this is a form of brute-force attack because you're just trying every combination to see if you can finally break into the application. Some other attacks you need to know birthday attacks. This attempts to find a high likelihood of hash collisions. So again, this is a type of brute-force attack as well. And we're looking to find similar or the same hashes from different inputs. Now, the birthday attack we discussed earlier on in domain three, this attack really is focused on what's called the birthday paradox. And this has to do with math calculations of if there's a certain amount of people in the room, there's a 50% chance they'll have the same birthday, that kind of stuff. You don't need to know that for the exam. What's important is that the idea behind the birthday paradox is, there is a possibility that there will be a hash collision at some point, and this attack focuses on leveraging that. This might help to lead to the discovery of a desired password. There's also social engineering where an attacker just basically tricks you into giving up your password. They call in as a system administrator, they call in as a manager or something like that, and they trick you into giving up a password so that they can get unauthorized access. Now, in terms of the tools that I talked about, these are called password recovery tools, and I'm using air quotes, but really they're password crackers, that's the idea behind them. So there's tools like Cain and Abel, there's John the Ripper, there's MimiKatz, there's HashCat, there's AirCrack, there's Hydra, there's Rainbow Crack, LophtCrack, and OphCrack, and there's many, many more. Now, Cain and Abel is focused on Windows that really helps to crack Windows credentials. John the Ripper will do multiple platforms, so it will do Windows and Unix, Linux-based systems. MimiKatz is Windows focused. HashCat will do multiple platforms. AirCrack is wireless network, so it's really focused on cracking web and WPA passwords. You have Hydra, which is focused on network, so it can crack HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, other passwords like that that are used for network based services. You have Rainbow Crack, and then we have LophtCrack, and we also have OphCrack. And both of those are Windows based credentials. So you can see a pattern here that windows is attacked pretty regularly 'cause there's a lot of tools, but these are the tools that you could possibly use to execute some of these attacks. Now, to defend against some of these attacks, first and foremost, we want to have strong, complex passwords. The more complex and the stronger the password is, the harder it's going to be for those tools to break. And this has been proven over and over throughout the industry, that the longer the password, the harder it will be to crack. Now, a strong password will contain at least one of each of the following characters, uppercase, lowercase, number, special character, one uppercase, one lowercase, one number, and one special character. When I create passwords, I always have two, two uppercase, two lowercase, two numbers, and two special characters. Strong passwords are also typically eight characters long. There are regulations and industry standards that say they need to be longer, 16 characters all the way up to 24 characters. So it's important to know what does FISMA require, what does HIPAA require, what does PCIDSS require, and so on. So we want to know those, that way when we create our password policy, we can define what that strong complex password is required to be. We also want to set a minimum and maximum password age that's got to be established in a policy somewhere. So minimum aging prevents password reuse, maximum also prevents that reuse, but it requires users to change their password in a specified amount of time. And also setting a password history will prevent the user from using older passwords, that way if they are compromised and they're in some dictionary file somewhere, or someone has a password file that they're using, those passwords will no longer be valid on the system as well. So again, passwords must be strong, complex, and they have to be updated regularly. And here's an example of what a complex password would look like. And again, one upper, one lower, one number one special character, that's the minimum. So here in this example, you have your uppercase, you have your number, you have your special character, and you have your lowercase. But notice how I have another uppercase, a couple more lower cases, and then another lowercase. Now, could I have changed the O to a zero? Yes, of course. This is really up to your creativity on how you want to create these passwords. But the idea is that you make it hard for an attacker to crack them using tools and also manually guessing them using brute-force methods. So the bottom line for password attacks is to know each one of these attacks and understand the password management techniques as well.```

Here is a structural summary of the video transcript on **Password Attacks**:

## 1. Introduction & Context
- Builds on previous video about single & multi-factor authentication.
- Password = secret credential (something you know) used to authenticate an identity (username).

## 2. Types of Passwords Mentioned
- **Standard password**: secret character code, passphrase, PIN.
- **Cognitive password**: answers to security questions (e.g., pet’s name, birthplace) used in self-service password reset.

## 3. Password Attack Types

| Attack | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Brute-force attack** | Attempt every possible character combination (umbrella category). |
| **Dictionary attack** | Uses a file of common words, known passwords, or decrypted passwords (tools: Hashcat, John the Ripper). |
| **Password spraying** | Single password tried against many different usernames (avoids account lockout). |
| **Credential stuffing** | Automated injection of stolen username/password pairs into login forms. |
| **Birthday attack** | Exploits hash collisions (birthday paradox) to find matching hashes from different inputs. |
| **Social engineering** | Tricking user into revealing password (e.g., impersonating admin/manager). |

## 4. Password Cracking Tools (Password “Recovery” Tools)

| Tool | Focus |
|------|-------|
| Cain & Abel | Windows credentials |
| John the Ripper | Windows, Unix, Linux |
| Mimikatz | Windows |
| Hashcat | Multi-platform |
| Aircrack | Wireless (WEP/WPA) |
| Hydra | Network services (HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, etc.) |
| RainbowCrack | Windows credentials |
| L0phtCrack / OphCrack | Windows credentials |

## 5. Defenses Against Password Attacks

- **Strong, complex passwords**:
  - Minimum: 1 uppercase, 1 lowercase, 1 number, 1 special character.
  - Longer passwords = harder to crack (8–24+ chars depending on regulation).
- **Password policy controls**:
  - Minimum & maximum password age (prevents reuse, forces regular changes).
  - Password history (prevents reuse of old/compromised passwords).
- **Regulatory awareness**: FISMA, HIPAA, PCI DSS requirements.

## 6. Bottom Line for Exam
- Know each attack type.
- Understand password management techniques.

```Welcome to this section of the course on Security Tests and Assessments. In this section, we're going to learn all about the critical role of testing, assessing, and auditing, and maintaining the integrity and security of information systems. Security tests and assessments aren't just technical exercises. They are a vital part of ensuring that an organization's policies and their procedures actually work in practice. And in the context of the CISSP exam, understanding security tests and assessment strategies is crucial because it ties directly into how security professionals validate systems and functionality. So whether it's through collecting security data, conducting audits, or validating disaster recovery plans, this is where the rubber meets the road when it comes to security operations. So in this first lesson of this section, we're going to look at how to plan for a Security Test and Assessment. And exam objective 6.1 of the CISSP exam outline states that you must know how to design and validate assessment, test, and audit strategies. And also objective 6.5 states that you need to be able to conduct and facilitate security audits. So we will cover both of these objectives in this particular lesson. From there, we'll then move on and discuss Performance and Risk Indicators. This lesson is focused on exam objective 6.3, which states that you need to know how to collect security process data. And in this lesson we'll focus on identifying key performance indicators or KPIs, and key risk indicators or KRIs from this data. These indicators help you monitor the effectiveness of your security controls, and assess potential risks before they escalate into incidents. Next, we'll shift our focus to collecting security process data, which is a crucial part of monitoring and maintaining a secure environment. The data you collect to support a test or assessment can make or break your results. So the data you collect can range from system logs, access control lists, to account management details and training compliance records as well. And in the following lessons, we will focus on the specific types of data that you need to know for the exam. You'll learn how to gather Account Management Data, which includes monitoring user accounts, roles, and privileges to ensure that the principle of lease privilege is being followed and it's being applied properly. We'll also look at Verifying Training and Awareness, which is another key aspect of collecting security data. It's one thing to have policies in place, but are your employees actually following those policies? Are they following them as they've been laid out? So in this lesson, we will focus on understanding the culture of security across the organization. And finally, we will explore Disaster Recovery and Business Continuity Data. As a security professional, you must ensure that the organization can recover from a disaster and continue to operate without losing sensitive information or causing any excessive downtime. So this lesson will walk you through the different types of data you need to collect and validate to ensure that your disaster recovery and business continuity plans are robust and effective. And to finish things off in this section, we will take a short quiz to see what you learned before we move on. So we're going to cover a lot of great stuff for domain six in this section. So when you're ready, let's dive into security tests and assessments. We'll get started with Security Test and Assessment Planning, and I'll see you there.```

```Welcome to this video on Security Test and Assessment Planning. In this video, we're going to focus on how to plan a security test or a security assessment, and do that from an internal, external, and third party perspective. Now, security professionals are often asked to participate in this, and that's why it's so important that you're familiar with these concepts. Now, a security test and assessment is basically designed to verify that security controls provide the proper level of security protection. So test, assessments, and audits. They're all designed to verify security controls provide the proper level of security. They just have a different purpose. So one thing to know is that these terms are often used interchangeably in the industry. Oftentimes, a test is really an assessment, and an assessment is really just a test. In the end, you're not going to be tested on this particular aspect. What you need to understand is the importance, the strategy, and the execution of a security test or assessment. Now, a security test ensures that a specific security control is functioning as designed. So this is conducted at regular intervals to test control performance, and also the effectiveness as well. So really, what we're looking to do is test a very specific function. Whatever that is, okay? It could be administrative, technical, or physical controls, doesn't really matter. But at the end of the day, we're focusing in on one specific function. And that allows us to identify the flaws within that specific function. That way, we can fix or address the security control concerns. Whereas a security control assessment is analyzing the security risk of a system component, application, or function. So a test is focused on the actual performance or effectiveness of the control, whereas now, we're looking at the risk associated with the control, and that's what the assessment is all about. We're looking at the overall security posture with organizational policy. So we're verifying that security controls and the security posture is meeting the organizational policy. So assessments are much more in depth than a test is. So we're looking to verify controls, change management processes, baselines, configurations, policies, and so on. And we often generate a report from this to provide to our senior managers or our stakeholders. So we're not just looking at functionality here, we're looking at the complete analysis of the security posture. Then we write these reports, and they are often written at an executive level to help senior managers understand how to make risk decisions. So let's compare the two in just kind of a practical scenario. Let's say we have a server, okay? If we wanted to perform a security test, we would do an inspection test. We would inspect a certain configuration or an misuse or abuse test, right? Where we're simulating system use and abuse against a certain function. Maybe we have manual procedures, maybe we have automated scripts that do this and so on. Or we can test the interface, like the network interface card, the NIC card. We can test an API, application programmable interface. We can test a lot of different things, even user interfaces, right? The application might have a user interface. Maybe we're testing that for injection attacks or something like that, right? This is a test to see how the server is going to respond according to those security controls. Whereas an assessment is going to go much deeper in terms of a vulnerability assessment, right? We're not looking at vulnerabilities for one specific thing. We're looking at vulnerabilities across the board, right? We're looking at them from an operating system perspective on the server, right? Maybe this server's running Linux of some kind, and then it's got multiple apps installed. So we're looking at vulnerabilities in those apps. We're looking at Linux overall. We're looking at all the functions, the services, the configurations, and so on. And then what if we're doing a risk assessment, right? If we're doing a risk assessment, that's going to be part of an overall organizational assessment. So we're including this server as part of that assessment. Same with the SCA or security control assessment. This would be part of an overall assessment. So you can see how the security test is much more focused and narrow, where the security assessment is more broad. And that's really the difference. Now, when coming up with a strategy for how you want to decide whether it's a test or an assessment or whatever it might be, the first thing that we want to do is to find the scope, right? What's in scope here? Are we only looking at this server? Is this server new? And are we deploying it to a new environment? Well, if it is, then maybe we want to just do a test, okay? But if it's part of a new install, and this server's going to be part of a new install for a data center, let's say, well, maybe that server needs to be compliant. So now we need to actually do an assessment because we have to prove compliance, okay? So that's going to really define what you choose to do here. And also, you want to understand the impact of a failed security control during the test or assessment. So what happens if the security control fails, right? How big of an impact is that? Is this a critical business function? Is it a critical business asset? Right? If those things are part of the concern, then maybe we don't want to do a test, we want to do an assessment so that we fully understand what we're dealing with. And we often want to identify what resources and personnel we need in order to execute the test or assessment. So what do we need to ensure that we have a successful test or assessment? Not just security, but everyone, administrators, because we often don't have root or administrative privileges. We need an administrator. What about an engineer or a manager? What about a software developer? Right? There's applications, we might need tools, licenses. Maybe we need to buy something to execute this test. So we need to identify those things as well. And this is important because oftentimes, this process is so unorganized from an approach perspective. So I've seen it many times in my career where everyone seems to think we just run a couple scanners like Nessus or OpenVAS or something like that, and that's good and great. We've got the scan reports, and that's enough. But what about the technical controls? What about the administrative controls and the physical controls that are all missed by these scanners, right? So we need to actually define all the scope, the objectives. We need to understand the impact of a failed control, because that's going to help us dial in and focus on what security controls we really want to test or assess. Plus, we also need resources and people to help us execute this, right? So that is part of the strategy. We also want to define the test criteria. What's going to constitute a success or a failure? From start to finish, what needs to be done here? What is the best way to execute this test procedure or this assessment? And understand what's going to be success or failure? And by documenting this and creating a solid plan, this will gain approval from your senior managers from a time, money, and effort perspective, right? Because it's going to take time and money to execute this procedure. So the idea is to make sure that everything is in place to conduct this test and make the most of what time, money, and effort is invested. We want to help the organization. We don't want to just go through the motions. We want to add value here from this exercise. Okay? So this is your test and assessment strategy. Now, let's talk about audits. Audits are assessments, but really what we're doing with an audit is we're using an independent body, an independent entity, and that gives us an impartial view of the overall results, right? When we're doing the test, when we're doing the assessment, we can kind of cheat, right? We can overlook things or we can fix things real quick, then retest it and say, now it's fixed. Well, the audit gives you an independent perspective, and you will know exactly what security controls are faulty, which ones are successful and effective, right? And this will be conducted as part of a compliance audit, maybe a security effectiveness audit, a security assessment audit, whatever you want to call it, right? That's what we're trying to accomplish here. And these audit reports are typically focused on compliance with governance, regulations, and it will compare it against the overall security posture. So whereas an assessment is focused on, "Hey, we could probably do better against this policy here, or we could have better defenses here." The audit is designed to give you an unbiased look at where you stand from a compliance perspective. So the report is more of a, you're compliant or non-compliant, and the perceived risk impact is also included in this report. Now, from an a security audit perspective, configuration management or change control is probably the most important aspect of this, because if you identify security controls that have failed, your change control process is probably the reason they fail, right? Yes, there's emerging threats, and yes, there's new vulnerabilities and that kind of stuff. I get that part. But from a change perspective, this is what we're talking about. We need to have a good solid configuration management and change control policy to make sure that our security controls remain effective throughout the lifecycle until we intend them to change, or we discover a new threat or vulnerability from one of our assessments or something like that. Okay? Now, you can do an internal audit, which is performed by internal organizational personnel. They don't report to anyone. They report straight to senior managers, and they perform this audit from a third party perspective. So this is typically like a self-audit before you're going to do an external audit. So how we end up doing this is you'll have internal auditors. They'll look at the computers, they'll look at servers, they'll look at network devices, whatever's in scope for this audit, and they will report directly to an executive officer in the company, whether it's a CEO, a CIO, CISO, whatever it is, they will report straight to them. The auditors will not engage with security managers, officers, engineers, or anything. They will go straight to executive officers. Whereas in an external audit, you have an outside organization that comes in and they specialize in security audits of whatever con you're looking for. This will eliminate the conflict of interest because you're an insider, you have a little bit of ownership here if you find security controls that are weak. So if you bring an outsider in, they have no influence, they have no bias. It doesn't matter to them what they find. So now, they're going to give you a true and accurate view of the security posture. Now, there are tons of firms that do this, okay? There's a lot of companies that specialize in this. And what they will do is they will come in and they will look at the computers, the servers, the networks, the databases, whatever it is, they will report to the executive officer as well, but they will also recruit from security management, security officers, and they will gather a team of individuals to help with that as well. So it's important to understand that the auditors are talking straight to senior managers. There's nobody else in between because we do not want to influence the reporting of the audit results. A third party audit is a little bit different. A third party audit is when you're bringing an outside team in, but it's on behalf of another organization, meaning another organization wants to know what your security posture is like. Now, this is typically performed for compliance purposes. Maybe there's a contractual agreement in place that says you need to do this, or as part of a corporate acquisition, you're buying another organization or you're buying a company at bringing them in. So how this works is the third party organization will come in and they will do their assessment against the computers, the servers, and all that. Right? Now, instead of reporting to an executive officer, they're going to report directly to an outside organization, whoever it is that wants this audited, okay? That eliminates that executive layer and also prevents influencing the reporting results or the audit results. Then the outside organization will discuss the results with the audited organization. So you can see how the third party remains kind of neutral in this process, and the accrediting body is what it's called. They will be looking to that third party audit team to conduct this and provide the results straight back to them. So the bottom line for this video is to know the difference between a security test and assessment. Know the purpose of a security audit, and also know the types of audits that we discussed in this video.```

Here is a structural summary of the video transcript on **Security Test and Assessment Planning**:

## 1. Core Concepts & Purpose
- **Goal:** Verify security controls provide the proper level of protection.
- **Key Distinction:** Terms (test, assessment, audit) are often used interchangeably, but they have different purposes.
- **Focus:** Importance, strategy, and execution—not terminology.

## 2. Security Test vs. Security Assessment

| Aspect | Security Test | Security Assessment |
|--------|---------------|---------------------|
| **Focus** | Specific function of a control | Overall risk of a system/component/application |
| **What it verifies** | Performance & effectiveness of a control | Security posture against organizational policy |
| **Depth** | Narrow, specific | Broad, in-depth |
| **Output** | Identifies flaws in one function | Report for senior managers/stakeholders on risk decisions |
| **Example (Server)** | Test NIC, API, UI, injection attacks, misuse/abuse | Vulnerability assessment across OS, apps, services; risk assessment; SCA |

## 3. Test & Assessment Strategy
Key planning elements:
- **Scope:** What is included? (e.g., new server vs. compliance requirement)
- **Impact of failure:** Critical business function/asset?
- **Resources & personnel:** Administrators, engineers, developers, tools, licenses
- **Test criteria:** Define success/failure, best execution method
- **Approval:** Document plan to gain senior manager buy-in (time, money, effort)

> **Note:** Avoid just running scanners (e.g., Nessus, OpenVAS)—include administrative, technical, and physical controls.

## 4. Security Audits (a type of assessment)
- **Key feature:** Independent body → impartial view
- **Purpose:** Compliance with governance/regulations; report = compliant/non-compliant + risk impact
- **Critical aspect:** Configuration management & change control (often root cause of failed controls)

### Types of Audits
| Type | Who performs | Reports to | Key characteristic |
|------|--------------|------------|--------------------|
| **Internal** | Internal personnel (no reporting line to security managers) | Executive officer (CEO, CIO, CISO) | Self-audit before external audit |
| **External** | Outside organization | Executive officer (may recruit internal help) | Eliminates conflict of interest |
| **Third-party** | Outside team (on behalf of another organization) | Outside organization (accrediting body) | For compliance, contracts, or acquisitions; neutral |

## 5. Bottom Line (Key Takeaways)
1. Know the **difference** between a security test and a security assessment.
2. Understand the **purpose** of a security audit.
3. Know the **types of audits** (internal, external, third-party).

```Welcome to this video on Performance and Risk Indicators. When performing a security assessment or test, you need something that's going to identify a potential failure or a potential success, and that's what we call indicators, and what we're looking for specifically are key performance indicators and key risk indicators. Now, the performance indicators and risk indicators are just measurements. It's measurements of success, or the lack of success, for security performance. Now, the KPIs, or key performance indicators, is the measurement of security performance, whereas the risk indicator is the measurement of known security risks. So, what we're looking for here is the ineffectiveness or potential failure of a security control, and that's where the risk indicator comes in. So, now the risk is, what's not working well and does this new risk pose a threat to the organization? So, some measurement examples we can reference are things like the results from a risk assessment or risk analysis, certainly vulnerability assessment test results, security assessment test procedure results, security incident occurrences, and patch level compliance. All of these can introduce measurements. How are the results from risk? When we do a quantitative or qualitative risk assessment, what were the results? What was the outcome, right? When we did a vulnerability assessment, how many vulnerabilities did we find, and are they critical? Are they high, are they moderate, are they low? And those are going to give you indications of were our patch levels are, right, because maybe we're unpatched. We haven't applied patches in a good sequence, or we don't have a good process for that, so now we identify another problem. So, the performance indicator is that we are not patching the system. Our performance is low in that regard, and it's increasing the key risk of the fact that we have vulnerabilities on the system, right? And same with the assessment procedures. Are we finding the same things over and over? Are accounts stale, meaning they're inactive and unprotected? Are accounts not being deprovisioned when they're supposed to? When, you know, personnel are terminated from the company, does it take us, you know, a couple days to deactivate the account? These are performance indicators. We're either performing or we're not, right? And then, certainly security incidents will be a huge factor in this. How did we respond to this incident? How fast did we recover from this incident? Did we do all the proper procedures in terms of collecting evidence, storing evidence, maintaining a proper chain of custody, all those things. These will be indicators of how we're doing from a security perspective. We can also get these in real time from our security information and event manager, our SIEM, something like Splunk or AlienVault, and so on. These will give you indicators. We can build dashboards to collect system logs, and we can start looking at various areas that we're concerned about, whether it be accounts, whether it be logins, whether it be threats or vulnerabilities. Whatever it is, we can configure these dashboards based on the information we're collecting from the systems to demonstrate that. For example, you have a box right here that's looking at your service level agreement. So, we're looking at all the different controls in which we're supposed to be compliant with a service level agreement. If we dip below, then we're lacking in performance and increasing our risk. If we're above, then we're increasing our performance and reducing our risk, okay? So, that's what we're looking at here. So, there's a couple different guides that you can reference just to get familiar with this. The one that I recommend is the NIST Special Publications 800-55. This is Performance Measurement Guide for Information Security. There's also the ISO 27004, Monitoring, measurement, analysis, and evaluation, and you can also reference ITIL for security management as well, and ITIL stands for Information Technology Infrastructure Library, okay? Now, for the exam, this is all you need to know about risk indicators. It's just understanding what they provide and how we're going to use them as part of a security test and assessment. So, the bottom line is just to understand the purpose of KPIs and KRIs, and also understand the metric measurement options.```

Here’s a structural summary of the video transcript on **Performance and Risk Indicators**:

---

### 1. **Purpose of Indicators**
- Used during security assessments/tests to identify potential **failure** or **success**.
- Two main types:
  - **Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)** – Measure *security performance* (success or lack thereof).
  - **Key Risk Indicators (KRIs)** – Measure *known security risks* (ineffectiveness or potential failure of controls).

---

### 2. **Measurement Examples**
- Risk assessment/analysis results (quantitative or qualitative).
- Vulnerability assessment results (number & severity of vulnerabilities).
- Security assessment test procedure results.
- Security incident occurrences (response time, recovery, evidence handling).
- Patch level compliance.

---

### 3. **Interplay Between KPIs & KRIs**
- Example: Low patching frequency → **KPI** shows poor performance → increases vulnerabilities → **KRI** shows elevated risk.

---

### 4. **Real-Time Monitoring**
- Via **SIEM** (e.g., Splunk, AlienVault).
- Dashboards can track:
  - Account status (stale, not deprovisioned after termination).
  - Logins, threats, vulnerabilities.
  - **SLA compliance** – below SLA = poor performance + increased risk; above SLA = good performance + reduced risk.

---

### 5. **Reference Guides**
- **NIST SP 800-55** – Performance Measurement Guide for Information Security.
- **ISO 27004** – Monitoring, measurement, analysis, evaluation.
- **ITIL** – Security management (IT Infrastructure Library).

---

### 6. **Exam Takeaway**
- Understand **purpose** of KPIs and KRIs.
- Know **metric measurement options** (what can be measured and how).

```Welcome to this video on collecting security data. As part of a security test or assessment, we need to collect certain types of data that will help us perform our security assessment or our security test. And we also want to have that data as evidence so that we can get management approval based on the results. Now, the data that we're going to collect is really just all of the output data that's generated by all of our security controls. A lot of the security controls we implement will generate some type of data or some type of output, and that's what we want to collect. And why this is important is for us to have a successful test assessment or a successful audit, this is all going to be dependent on the inputs that we provide to those tests, to those assessments, and to those audits. So we need to collect that data based on the purpose and the scope of whatever we're trying to test or assess. Now, when you perform a security test or an assessment, you're going to find that the quality is going to depend on one of three things. It's going to depend on the scope of what you're trying to test, the time you have to test it, and the cost it's going to take to test it. So, this is basically a project management principle called the triple constraint. If any of these are impacted, if time is impacted, cost is impacted or scope is impacted, then your quality's going to be impacted. So what we have to determine is what we're really trying to accomplish with that security test. So basically, if any of these sides of the triangle are affected, the two other areas are going to be affected as well, and these constraints will apply 100% to the quality. So the more data we collect, the scope, the more time and money the assessment will cost, right? But if the test needs to be done quickly, then the more resources we need to throw at this, cost, and the scope is going to have to decrease because we're going to have to get this done quickly, right? So there really needs to be a good balance in the quality overall, the scope, and we need to understand the time and cost impacts as well. That's going to determine what kind of data we need to collect to make the test the best it could possibly be. And the first place we want to start is collecting any administrative data. So we want to gather our policies, processes, procedures and any other documentation. So we want to look for records, logs, other archive data, any of those different things that can help demonstrate completion or compliance in terms of the security controls or any other previous security assessments as well. So we can use all of that information as part of our current test and assessment. And make sure that you're considering other departments as well. Finance departments, human resources, those kinds of things. They might have relevant data that might be needed for the assessment. Then we need to collect our technical data, so our system logs, software code, configuration files, change management records or change control board files, things like that. Also our logical and technical data as well. And we want to review system diagrams and other system related documentation that are going to define the technical specifications for systems operations. So we want to be looking at the current diagrams, we want to look at data flow diagrams if we can. We want to understand exactly what we're trying to test and what we expect as the outcome. Once we understand all of that, then we need to go to our management, our senior managers, or whoever's going to sponsor this test or assessment because these tests are going to rely heavily on their support because we can't do them by ourselves. So we need managers to allocate resources to put towards these tests and assessments, whether it be administrators, engineers, architects and so on. We also want to make sure that they clearly understand the purpose and scope of these tests and assessments so that the proper resources are allocated to help us complete this in terms of the time, the cost, and the scope of what we're trying to accomplish. The approval needs to be formally documented. We need to have this documented in a policy, a procedure, or if it's part of a change control board process or whatever it might be. But we want to get this formally approved and formally documented. We also want to clearly identify the expected outcomes, the schedule of what we're going to do with the test, what the expected start dates, end dates, start times, end times, all those things, the risk exceptions, anything that's out of scope, we want to document that, and any other information that should be part of the documentation. In other words, we want to thoroughly, methodically plan this test out and get full management approval for it. So the bottom line is to understand the purpose of collecting the process data. Know to collect administrative and technical data, And also know that management support and approval are needed for a successful test or assessment.```

```Welcome to this video on Account Management Data. When performing a security assessment or a security test, it's very important to include accounts, specifically identities and authenticators as a part of the security assessment or the security test. Now, the account management data, just make sure that authorized subjects are maintaining the proper privilege levels, right? We're trying to avoid authorization or privilege crete. So these accounts are their credentials that are used to access the system. So it's a user's identity and their authenticators. So to test and assess the system, we primarily want to look at the account management lifecycle. Now that account management lifecycle starts with creation, how accounts are created, how those credentials are created. So this could be a part of our test when we perhaps go through a procedure that a system administrator might follow. How do the accounts get created? What are the approval processes? How are we actually doing this from a logical perspective within Active Directory, LDAP, RADIUS, TACACS, all those different components that we might have to use. Also, how are accounts being modified? When we update those accounts to provision, add new privileges or de-provision, remove privileges, how is that done? Where is that logged? How is that captured? All those different things need to be taken in account when we're performing an assessment or test. And are we auditing those accounts to detect privilege or permission or authorization creep? And are we deleting those accounts, or revoking or removing those accounts according to organizational regulations, organizational policy, and so on. So let's dive a little deeper into each one of these steps just in case you see a question on the exam, starting with the creation of accounts. So what we want to do first is we want to acquire a list of the system accounts from all of our centralized, Active Directory, LDAP, RADIUS, TACACS, et cetera, or all of our local authentication services. That way we can look at our admin accounts, our route accounts, and some of our, what we call brick glass, or emergency accounts as well. And we want to review that list, right? We want to see if there's authorized or unauthorized accounts on this list. And we also want to maybe look at the system logs to see when these accounts were created and if there's one specific administrator who's creating them all, because maybe we have an insider that we need to be concerned with as well, right? So as part of a test and assessment, this might help uncover an insider threat or a security incident as well. Same with the modifications. We want to review those log files to ensure the account actions are being captured correctly. When privileges are being added, provisioning when privileges are being removed, de-provisioning, is this getting logged? And perhaps one of our procedures is something we execute to demonstrate logging and prove that we are actually capturing this information as part of our logging process. And then with auditing, we want to review these accounts to ensure proper privilege levels are assigned to each account. And we don't want to do this as just part of a test and assessment, we want to do this regularly, or periodically depending on your policy. So normally we're going to do this annually, you're at least going to look through the accounts no matter what's going on in the organization, you want to look at your accounts at least annually, but it's going to depend on your industry and the regulation. So there could be a more often frequency in terms of maybe monthly, every quarter, every six months, whatever it might be. Then we want to identify any remediations. So if we identify some accounts that are non-compliant, maybe we have an account that's been inactive for a little while and it's not disabled, we want to recommend it gets disabled. If maybe we have a disabled account that we've had for years, maybe we want to recommend archiving that account or deleting that account. So it all depends on the industry and the regulation as well. And then when it comes to deleting accounts, we want to recommend accounts for access revocation, or deprovisioning, or deletion based on the audit findings. So if we're performing a test assessment or we're auditing these accounts, we want to identify those problematic accounts. Maybe we're revoking access, or maybe this account has been around for long enough, and according to our governance regulations and compliance requirements, we want to delete them. Now, normally a regulation is going to dictate you need to maintain an account for a certain period of time. Maybe it's three years, maybe it's five years, or seven years, whatever it is. And we want to identify those accounts when the time comes to delete them, because we do not want to maintain any data whatsoever for any longer than we absolutely have to. So the bottom line for this video is to understand each step of the account management lifecycle as it pertains to security test and assessments.```

Here is a structural summary of the video on **Account Management Data**:

## 1. Core Concept
- Accounts (identities + authenticators) are critical components of security assessments.
- Goal: Ensure authorized subjects maintain proper privilege levels and avoid privilege creep.

## 2. Key Focus: Account Management Lifecycle
The lifecycle consists of four main stages:

### A. Creation
- Obtain a list of system accounts (centralized: AD, LDAP, RADIUS, TACACS; local auth services).
- Review for authorized/unauthorized accounts.
- Examine logs for creation details (e.g., single admin creating all accounts → possible insider threat).

### B. Modification
- Review logs to verify account actions are captured correctly.
- Check that provisioning (adding privileges) and de-provisioning (removing privileges) are logged.
- Execute procedures to demonstrate logging effectiveness.

### C. Auditing
- Regularly (annually or per policy/regulation) review accounts for proper privilege levels.
- Frequency depends on industry/regulation (monthly, quarterly, semi-annually).
- Identify non-compliant accounts (e.g., inactive but not disabled → recommend disable; long-disabled → archive or delete).

### D. Deletion / Revocation
- Recommend access revocation, de-provisioning, or deletion based on audit findings.
- Follow governance/regulatory retention periods (e.g., 3, 5, 7 years).
- Delete accounts when retention expires to avoid unnecessary data retention.

## 3. Bottom Line
Understand each step of the account management lifecycle as it applies to security testing and assessments.

```Welcome to this video on, Verifying Training and Awareness. When performing a Security Assessment or a Security Test, as part of your data collection for the security processes, part of this is going to be administrative controls, so we wanted to include Training and Awareness, as part of that. Now, Training and Awareness, is all about bringing relevant security matters to employee's attention, or to personnel's attention. We want to raise awareness to the foundational requirements that are needed in terms of security practices within the organization. So the goal is to make sure that personnel are aware of their responsibilities as it pertains to security within the organization. And Security Training is about teaching people how to perform their duties and do it securely. So as part of the assessment, we want to take a look at the Training Records. We want to gather personnel training records that map to training objectives. So if we have an objective, say we're running really high in terms of phishing attacks, we're getting a lot of phishing attacks, and personnel are clicking on links like they're not supposed to. So then we create a little training program to make sure that we educate folks on what to do and how to respond to those phishing emails. So what we want to do is look at the key risk indicators and key performance indicators from that training, and we want to understand compliance requirements for each of the training objectives as well. Now, keep in mind when you collect this data, make sure that this data does not have any sensitive information, such as their employee numbers or anything that you can uniquely identify them, and we want to handle those accordingly. So those training objectives are going to determine if security is being met through the current training materials and methods. Remember way back into domain one, when we talked about personnel, when we're onboarding personnel, bringing them into the organization, training is a part of that, and we want to train them in their responsibilities and their duties from a security perspective. So this is our chance to test and assess to make sure we're doing the right things from a training perspective. We also want to identify any kind of emerging threats, any new vulnerabilities or any other risks that are not present in the current training materials. This is part of due care and diligence, right? Due care is that we created a training program. Due diligence is that we're updating the training program to reflect the new threats, vulnerabilities, and risks that are out there. We also want to make sure that people are actually attending these trainings. We want to identify any non-compliant personnel with current training requirements. So if we have people who are onboarding, we want to hold them accountable to complete the training within a certain amount of time. And we also want to identify any frequent offenders who violate security policy or do not complete the security training on time. And if we have those, the frequent offenders, we want to conduct remedial training, where we remediate non-compliance with any makeup sessions or on-demand training options. And we also want to consider revoking or removing privileges and access until they complete that training. So if we have personnel that onboard, or we have some frequent violators or offenders of security policy, if they continue to do it, part of their punishment is we deprovision their access until they complete it and satisfy the requirements. So the bottom line for this video is just to understand the importance of auditing, security training and awareness. It gives us overall situational awareness of how effective our training awareness programs are within the organization.```

Here is a structural summary of the video transcript on **Verifying Training and Awareness**:

### 1. Purpose & Context
- Part of **Security Assessment / Security Test** data collection.
- Focuses on **Administrative Controls** (Training & Awareness).

### 2. Key Definitions
- **Awareness:** Raising attention to foundational security requirements and employee responsibilities.
- **Training:** Teaching personnel how to perform duties *securely*.

### 3. Data Collection Focus: Training Records
- Map training records to specific **training objectives** (e.g., anti-phishing).
- Review **Key Risk Indicators (KRIs)** & **Key Performance Indicators (KPIs)**.

```Welcome to this video on Disaster Recovery and Business Continuity Data. When performing a security assessment or a security test, so long as it applies, it's important to consider the disaster recovery and business continuity data as part of this test or assessment. And also, we want to consider things like backup data, as well. Now, if you recall from previous videos, we've talked about business continuity a lot, so I don't want to go too far into it here, but business continuity is about assessing and minimizing the risks to critical business processes in the event of some kind of major disruption, and disaster recovery is the processes or procedures that are necessary to recover those critical business processes from a disruption. So a very simple way of thinking about it is business continuity is all about critical business functions. Disaster recovery, information technology. That's what we want to do with both of these. Now, as part of the assessment or the test, we want to make sure that we have copies of both the business continuity plan and the disaster recovery plan if they exist. Not every company has one, not every organization has one. Should they have them? Absolutely. Do they have them? Usually not. So we want to make sure that if we can get a copy of them, we do. We also want to know what were the results from the latest business continuity or disaster recovery test event. So if we did some kind of a test, such as a parallel test or a simulation test or whatever, we want to know what the results were, what were the outcomes of that. So if we get the business continuity plan or the disaster recovery plan, plus the results, and they're two years old, then we already know that we have some remediation work to do, right? And that's really what we're looking to do here. So as part of the tests, we can actually conduct a disaster recovery test along with our security assessment, as well. If you recall from the previous video, there's a checklist test, which basically every member of the team is going to get a copy of this. They're going to look through it, provide the review and their comments. This is also called a read through test, as well. There's also a structured walkthrough test where all team members review the plan together in a conference room or in a meeting room of some kind, and that helps us identify any issues. This is also called a tabletop exercise in reference to everyone has the documents on the table, and we're just kind of walking through it. Now, what was the outcome of this, right? ### 1. Core Concepts
- **Business Continuity (BC):** Assessing and minimizing risks to *critical business processes* during major disruptions.
- **Disaster Recovery (DR):** Processes/procedures to *recover* those critical processes after a disruption.
- **Simple distinction:** BC = business functions; DR = information technology.

### 2. Key Documents & Artifacts to Review
- **BCP & DR Plan:** Obtain copies (if they exist). Many organizations lack them.
- **Latest test results:** Identify age (e.g., 2-year-old results indicate remediation needed).

### 3. Types of DR Tests (with assessment focus)
| Test Type | Description | Assessment Focus |
|-----------|-------------|------------------|
| **Checklist / Read-through** | Individual review of plan | Gaps in review/comments |
| **Structured walkthrough / Tabletop** | Team reviews together | Issues in controls, redundancy, high availability |
| **Simulation test** | Scenario-based (natural/manmade disaster) | Remedial steps identified & fixed |
| **Parallel test** | Execute procedures without impacting operations | Most attention needed; tests recovery site, no disruption |
| **Full interruption test** | Impact operations; move to recovery/cloud site | Verify controls, missing procedures/processes, logical/technical controls |

### 4. Backup Data Assessment
- **Gather:** tapes, discs, drives.
- **Test for:**
  - Proper retention requirements.
  - Archiving best practices (e.g., encryption at rest).
  - Recovery from potential data loss.
- **Review backup logs:** frequency, policy compliance, encryption at rest.

### 5. Backup Methods
- **Full backup:** Complete copy of all data (objects + user data).
- **Differential backup:** Data changed since last *full* backup.
- **Incremental backup:** Data changed since last *full* or *incremental* backup.

### 6. Key Validation Questions
- Can we recover from the full backup?
- Are differential/incremental backups correctly capturing modified data?
- Is rotation properly overwriting oldest data first, retaining most current?

### 7. Bottom Line (Learning Objectives)
- Understand the **purpose** of BC & DR testing.
- Know the **different DR tests**.
- Understand the **purpose of testing data backups**.
- Know the **different data backup methods**.

- **Goal:** Identify and categorize security flaws/weaknesses.

- NIST National Vulnerability Database (NVD)
- Mitre CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures)
- US-CERT

- **Developer:** NIST (see SP 800-126).

|----------|-----------|---------|
| **XCCDF** | Extensible Configuration Checklist Description Format | Security checklist/benchmark results (most common in the field) |
| **OVAL** | Open Vulnerability and Assessment Language | Configuration info, machine states, assessment results |
| **OCIL** | Open Checklist Interactive Language | Info from people or existing data stores (less common) |

|--------|-----------|---------|

| **SWID** | Software Identification | Software identifier + metadata |
| **CCE** | Common Configuration Enumeration | Dictionary of software security configurations |
| **CVE** | Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures | Security-related software flaws |

#### C. SCAP Scoring Systems
| System | Full Name | Purpose |
|--------|-----------|---------|

| **CCSS** | Common Configuration Scoring System | Severity for a configuration issue |

- OpenSCAP (Unix/Linux only)
- Tripwire
- Nessus (supports XCCDF & OVAL)
- InsightVM (Rapid7)

- Understand the **purpose** of a vulnerability assessment.
- Know **SCAP** and its **different components** (languages, schemes, scoring systems).

Here is a structural summary of the video transcript on **Vulnerability Scanning**:

### 1. Definition & Purpose
- **Vulnerability scanning** = using automated tools to identify and categorize security flaws (vulnerabilities).
- Common tools: Nessus, InsightVM, OpenVAS, Nmap, Qualys, Nikto (web server), Tripwire.

### 2. Types of Scans (by Access Level)
| Scan Type | Description | Outcome |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| **Non-credentialed** | Read-only, general user access | Fast but limited results |
| **Credentialed (Authenticated)** | Logs in with privileged credentials | Thorough scan: patching levels, configs, etc. |

### 3. Discovery Scans (e.g., with Nmap)
- **Goal**: Find active hosts on an IP range/subnet (not vulnerabilities).
- **Method**: SYN scan (“half-open” TCP handshake) – sends SYN, waits for SYN/ACK.
- **Port statuses**: Open, Closed, Unknown/Filtered (blocked by firewall/security).
- **Contrast**: TCP connect scan completes full handshake – slower but needed before vulnerability scanning.

### 4. Other Scan Techniques
- **ACK scan**: Sends ACK packet to test for firewalls (stateful vs. stateless) and filtered ports.
- **Xmas scan**: Sends PSH, URG, FIN flags (all except SYN/ACK) – hopes for a response.
- **UDP scan**: Checks UDP services (no handshake, connectionless).

### 5. Vulnerability Scanning Itself
- **How it works**: Compares target host against a **signature database** (patches, misconfigurations, open ports).
- **Scope**: Networks, applications, databases, OSes.
- **Output example (Nessus)**: Critical, High, Medium, Info findings (categorized by vendor – verify manually).
- **Post-scan actions**:
  - Analyze & prioritize findings (organizational policy, risk tolerance).
  - Rule out false positives.
  - Create assessment report + remediation strategy for management approval.

### 6. Important Operational Rules
- **Do NOT fix anything without approval** – can impact production, change control, operations.
- Follow organizational processes methodically.

### 7. Best Practices for Scanning
- **Communicate** clearly: what, when, how long.
- **Run during off-hours / low activity** to minimize business impact.
- **Keep scanners updated** with latest vendor signatures.
- **Scan small host groups** (e.g., /24 networks) – not large subnets like /8 or /16.
- **Test scanner configs/profiles** in dev/test/sandbox environments first.
- **Avoid tools that auto-apply remediations** – they can break production and lose previous state.

### 8. Bottom Line (Key Exam Points)
- Purpose of a vulnerability scan.
- Meaning of credentialed/authenticated scans.
- Different scan types (SYN, ACK, Xmas, UDP, connect).
- Scanning best practices.

## 1. Core Concept of Penetration Testing
- **Definition**: Simulates a system attack by attempting to exploit known or discovered vulnerabilities.
- **Scope**: Can be **physical** (locks, doors, guards, cameras) or **logical** (software, networks).

## 2. Rules of Engagement (ROE)
- **Definition**: An agreement defining how and why the test is conducted.
- **Key elements**:

## 3. Types of Penetration Tests
| Type | Also Known As | Knowledge Level | Cost |
|------|--------------|----------------|------|
| White box | Full-knowledge | All details known to testers | Cheapest |
| Black box | No/zero knowledge | No test details shared | Most expensive |
| Gray box | Partial knowledge | Some information provided, some withheld | Middle ground |

## 4. Penetration Testing Teams
- **Red Team**: Simulates the attacker.
- **Blue Team**: Defends against the attack (e.g., SOC, security analysts).
- **Purple Team**: Collaboration between red and blue teams to share information and strengthen security posture.

## 5. Breach and Attack Simulation (BAS)
- **Definition**: Automated testing to determine if security controls can detect and respond to threats.
- **Method**: Uses synthetic transactions and attack simulations (e.g., SYN scans, brute force attacks).

## 1. Overview & Context
- **Purpose of penetration testing**: Simulate a system attack from an attacker’s perspective to exploit known/discovered vulnerabilities.
- **Five core phases**: Discovery, Scanning, Exploitation, Post-Exploitation, Reporting.

## 2. Phase Details

### Phase 1: Discovery / Reconnaissance
- **Type**: Passive reconnaissance (undetected).
- **Methods**: OSINT, footprinting.
- **Goal**: Collect info about target without interacting with the system (avoid IDS, endpoint security).

### Phase 2: Scanning
- **Type**: Active reconnaissance (detectable).
- **Methods**: Ping sweeps, port scans, banner grabs, vulnerability scans, enumeration.
- **Goal**: Find vulnerabilities/weaknesses in network or system components.

### Phase 3: Exploitation
- **Action**: Bypass security controls (manual or automated tools like Metasploit).
- **Focus**: Execute customized/predefined attacks, avoid Indicators of Compromise (IoCs).
- **Goal**: Attack and exploit while staying undetected as long as possible.

### Phase 4: Post-Exploitation
- **Actions**:
  - Pivot / move laterally (east-west movement).
  - Maintain access for further discovery, scanning, exploitation.
  - Cover tracks: erase logs, remove files/scripts/rootkits.
- **Goal**: Maintain access and erase evidence of ethical hacking activity.

### Phase 5: Reporting
- **Executive summary**: High-level findings, impact on business, next steps.
- **Technical report**: Administrator/engineer view, remediation needs.
- **Contents**: Rules of engagement, step-by-step attack documentation (procedures, screenshots, videos), outcomes of all exploits (successes & failures).
- **Goal**: Document findings and recommended remediations.

## 3. Post-Test Cleanup (Not an official phase but recommended)
- Recover crashed/disrupted hosts.
- Remove tools, scripts, outputs to prevent unauthorized access or policy violations.
- Leave the system in the same condition as found.

## 4. Bottom Line
Clearly understand each phase and what happens during it.

## 1. **Definition & Purpose of Logs**
- A log is a **record** of system-related changes and events in **chronological order**.
- Also called **audit logs** or **audit trails** (used to audit system events).
- Captures specific actions: creations, modifications, deletions, logons, privileged access, user account management.

---

## 2. **Configuration & Standards**
- What gets logged is defined by **organizational policy** (regulations set minimum requirements).
- Key guidance documents:
  - **NIST SP 800-92** (Guide to Computer Security Log Management)
  - **ISO 27001 / 27002** (high-level logging guidance)

---

## 3. **Syslog Standard**
- **Syslog** = standardized format for consistent log data collection and transfer.
- Components:
  - **Facility codes** (e.g., 4 = auth/authorization, 10 = authpriv)
  - **Severity levels** (0 = most info, 7 = least info; typical = 5/Notice, 6/Info)
- **Weakness**: No built-in authentication → weak security.

---

## 4. **Clock Synchronization (NTP)**
- Critical for creating accurate **chronological audit trails**.
- **NTP (Network Time Protocol)** – port 123, UDP, connectionless.
- **Stratum clocks**:
  - Stratum 0: most accurate (GPS, atomic clocks, radio signals) – reference clock.
  - Stratum 1: network appliance connected to Stratum 0.
  - Stratum 2: individual computers.
  - **For logging, use Stratum 0 or 1** (not Stratum 2).

---

## 5. **Log Protection & Best Practices**
- Send logs to a **remote log server/repository** → prevents local tampering.
- Set **proper file/directory privileges** (read access allowed, no modification/deletion).
- Use **hashing** to ensure data integrity.
- Periodically **test and assess** log capabilities for compliance.

---

## 6. **Uses of Logs**
- Security testing, audits, assessments.
- Supports security controls, incident response, and troubleshooting.

---

## 7. **Exam Takeaways**
- Understand system logs and their purpose.
- Know **syslog** (standardized format, facility codes, severity levels).
- Know **clock synchronization (NTP, stratum levels)**.
- Know **log review security best practices** (remote storage, access control, integrity, testing).
