```Welcome to this video on configuration management. As part of security operations, it's important to understand configuration management and implement it properly. Configuration management are the activities that ensure that system components maintain a known configuration state. We want to make sure that there are never unauthorized changes to the system, and that's what we're focused on with configuration management. The configuration itself are just the specifications or settings of an asset. It's the configuration of a server, a workstation, a firewall, right? We're talking about the configuration. Those are the specifications, what's enabled, what's disabled, what's operating, what's not operating on these specific devices. It also has to do with architecture design, where interfaces are connecting, how they're connected up to switches or routers or firewalls, and all these different things. This is the configuration. The configuration item within CM is the asset that requires configuration control. We are controlling how the configuration is managed on these specific devices. Now, there's another topic, which is change control, and we will talk about that in the next video. And to manage all of this, we need a configuration management plan. This is going to define how the organization manages and controls configuration changes to these system assets. Now, most organizations will have a CM, a configuration management policy, or they'll have some kind of document that's going to outline what the organizational intention is for CM, how they comply with it, and so on. So this policy is really the intention, where the plan is the execution of the policy. That's why we need a plan. The plan is going to document all of the different aspects of configuration management, the purpose, the scope, the roles, the responsibilities, the processes and procedures, and all the stuff that goes into it. Then we're going to talk about, in the CM plan, talk about where everything gets managed and what products, what systems, the CIs, right, the configuration items, what we're actually going to be managing. So it's important to know that not everything needs to be configuration managed. Not everything's going to be a CI. Not everything's going to be controlled. Now, for the focus of the remainder of this video, we're going to discuss the NIST special publications 800-128. This is the Guide for Security-Focused Configuration Management of Information Systems, and there are four main phases of configuration management, and of course, everything's going to start with planning. We need to properly plan, and we need to lay everything out before we start enforcing configuration management. Now, the first thing that we have to do is identify all of the CIs, the configuration items, right? That's going to help us determine the scope of the overall configuration management plan. Then once we know the scope, we're going to create the CM policy, the processes, and the procedure for all of the configuration items that we want to control. Then we need to establish the change control board, or the CCB. The CCB are the group of individuals with the authority to review and approve a configuration item change. Once an item is change controlled, it can no longer be changed without the authorization of the CCB, and these are a group of whoever, right? It can be engineers, architects, administrators, managers. Anyone can be on the CCB, and this is totally up to your organization. The idea behind this is you need a good balance of people on this board. So typically, you're going to have designated members for sure that are specific to the CCB, but then you might have guest members as well. If there's a specific configuration item that's changing, you might want to bring in the subject matter expert for that item to speak to this change and the impact to the organization when it makes a change, right? So let's say your CCB has a bunch of system administrators. If you're making a network change, you're going to want to bring in a network engineer or a network architect who can speak intelligently to why this change is being made and how it's going to impact the overall security posture, and also how it's going to impact the organization, okay? Now, the CCB goes by a lot of different names. It might be a change advisory board, a CAB. It might be a change control board, which is CCB. There's a variety of names. At the end of the day, understand that you need a group of responsible people to review and approve these changes. That way, not one person is controlling it, right? What's one of the most important concepts about security operations? Separation of duties, right? Or segregation of duties. We don't want one individual controlling the configuration. We want a group of folks taking a look at things and authorizing them based on the organizational and security posture. We also want to make sure that all of these changes, the recommended changes, the request for changes, all those different things are documented. It needs to be well documented and tracked throughout the entire process. So once planning is complete, now we move over to identifying and implementing the different configurations. So what we're going to do now is define what that secure baseline configuration looks like. What is the secure baseline for all the CIs? How are the web servers configured? How are the network devices configured? And so on. This baseline configuration is the defined specification settings of a CI. So this is what's going to be referenced for future changes. That's why we call it the baseline, right? It's a version. It is the baseline. Now, when we make a change, we're going to update that baseline, and once that baseline's gone through the CM process and it's been formally reviewed and approved, now we upgrade or update that baseline to the new version, and those versions are going to be pre-configured CIs that are used to ensure consistent configuration is deployed. So if we're building a new firewall, if we're building a new web server or a new infrastructure server for some hypervisors, or whatever we're doing, we can refer back to, "Hey, what's the VMware baseline for vSphere? Oh, it's this. It's 1.5.6. Cool. Deploy that, right?" Because that's the approved baseline, and we know the risks inside that baseline. Does that make sense? That's what we're trying to accomplish. Here is a structural summary of the video transcript on **Configuration Management (CM)** :

### 1. Core Definition & Purpose
- **Configuration Management (CM):** Activities ensuring system components maintain a *known* configuration state.
- **Primary Goal:** Prevent unauthorized changes to systems.
- **Configuration:** Specifications/settings of an asset (server, firewall, etc.), including architecture design (interfaces, connections).

### 2. Key Terminology
- **Configuration Item (CI):** The asset that requires configuration control.
- **Change Control:** A related but separate topic (covered in next video).
- **CM Plan:** Defines *how* the organization manages/configures changes to assets.
- **CM Policy vs. Plan:** Policy = intention; Plan = execution (purpose, scope, roles, processes).

### 3. NIST SP 800-128 Framework (4 Phases)

| Phase | Key Activities |
|-------|----------------|
| **1. Planning** | Identify CIs (scope) → Create CM policy/processes → Establish a **Change Control Board (CCB)** (review/approve changes). CCB ensures separation of duties. |
| **2. Identifying & Implementing** | Define **secure baseline configuration** (specifications/version). Use versions for consistent deployment. **Provisioning** = create/manage/destroy CIs (can be automated via DevOps tools like Chef, Puppet, Ansible). |
| **3. Controlling** | Maintain secure baseline → Conduct security impact assessments for changes → Update CM plan & baseline documentation. |
| **4. Monitoring** | Analyze compliance with approved baselines (using integrity tools: AIDE, Tripwire, discovery/vulnerability scans). Identify unauthorized changes & improve CM processes. |

### 4. Important Concepts
- **Not everything is a CI** – only assets requiring control.
- **CCB composition:** Designated members + guest SMEs (e.g., network engineer for network changes).
- **Baseline versions** enable recovery, consistent deployment, and risk awareness.
- **Automation** (DevOps/DevSecOps) allows approved baselines to be provisioned without repeated security analysis.

### 5. Exam Takeaway
Understand the **purpose of CM**, key terms (CI, baseline, provision), and the **4-phase CM process** (Plan → Identify/Implement → Control → Monitor).

---

## 1. Definition & Purpose
- **Patch**: Fix for a known functionality problem in software/firmware (bug fixes, new features, security updates).
- **Patch Management**: Consistent process to identify and install patches while avoiding operational impact.
- **Link to Vulnerability Management**: Patches often fix vulnerabilities.

---

## 2. Key Policy & Process Elements
- **Patch management policy** must outline:
  - Identification, acquisition, installation, responsibilities.
  - Avoiding production/operations impact.
- **Key challenges**: timeliness, priority setting, testing before deployment.

---

## 3. When Patching Is Not Possible
- Options if a system/application cannot be patched:
  - Reconfigure (disable vulnerable service).
  - Remove the application.
  - Apply **compensating controls** (e.g., whitelisting, TLS encryption).
- Requires quick risk analysis.

---

## 4. Patch Management Architectures

| Approach | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| **Agent-based (centralized)** | Agents on hosts communicate with internal patch server → most common & effective. |
| **Agentless** | Server scans systems to detect missing patches. |
| **Passive network monitoring** | Monitors local network traffic to identify patching needs (limited to protocol-level visibility). |
| **Decentralized** | Hosts manage own patches → not recommended (loss of configuration control & baseline). |

- **NIST SP 800-40r3** comparison highlights: agent-based needs admin privileges, supports remote hosts, most effective overall.

---

## 5. General Steps of Patch Management
1. **Evaluate** – Identify relevant patches from trusted sources (e.g., NIST, vendors).
2. **Test** – Assess for negative impacts in sandbox/dev environment.
3. **Approve** – Submit to change control board (part of change/config management).
4. **Deploy** – Install in production as soon as possible to reduce risk exposure.
5. **Verify** – Confirm effectiveness and no operational issues (security tests, audits).

---

## 6. Bottom Line for Exam
- Understand **purpose & challenges** of patch management.
- Know **architectures** (agent-based vs. agentless vs. passive monitoring).
- Memorize the **5 general steps** (Evaluate → Test → Approve → Deploy → Verify).

## 1. Terminology & Relationship to Configuration Management
- **Change Management** and **Change Control** are interchangeable terms (NIST uses "change control").
- **Configuration Management (CM)** is the overarching 4-phase process:
  1. Planning
  2. Identifying & implementing configurations
  3. **Controlling configuration changes** ← Change control lives here
  4. Monitoring
- Change control applies to any **Configuration Item (CI)** : computer, app, server, firewall, mobile device, switch, router, etc.

## 2. The Change Control Process (7 Steps)

| Step | Action |
|------|--------|
| 1. **Request** | Formally request & record proposed change (ticket/form required for documentation) |
| 2. **Review** | Change Control Board (CCB) reviews impact |
| 3. **Build & Test** | Done in a development environment; identify security/functional impacts |
| 4. **Approve/Reject** | CCB decides based on test results (approve, approve with modifications, or reject) |
| 5. **Implement** | Deploy approved change without impacting **Ops** (government/federal) or **Prod** (commercial) – same meaning |
| 6. **Verify** | Confirm correct implementation; document new CI configuration |
| 7. **Close Out** | Update baseline, CM plan, all documentation → roll to new baseline version |

## 3. Flow of Roles
- **Requester** → documents change request
- **CCB** → reviews, then approves/rejects after testing
- **Engineers / Admins / Security Engineers** → build, test, implement
- **CCB** → final verification & close-out

## 4. Security Impact Analysis (Key Activities within Change Control)
- **Release control** – part of implementation step
- **Security impact analysis** includes:
  - Identify potential security risks/impacts
  - Discover vulnerabilities in software/hardware/assets affected by the change
  - Assess risks from threats/vulnerabilities
  - Assess impact on existing security/privacy controls and overall security posture
  - Perform **regression testing** (ensure change doesn't break other system parts)
- **Plan safeguards & countermeasures** – reduce risk to acceptable level (proactive + reactive)
- **Follow change control process** to update the security baseline (build security in early, not after deployment)

## 5. Bottom Line (Exam Focus)
- Know the **purpose** of change management/control
- Understand the **process** (request → review → build/test → approve → implement → verify → close out)
- Understand the **security impact analysis process**

Here is a structural summary of the provided video transcript on **Software Configuration Management (CM)** :

### 1. Core Definition & Purpose
- **Software CM** ensures software maintains a *known configuration*.
- Critical for large and enterprise-level environments.
- Focuses on the software side (vs. general CM covered elsewhere).

### 2. Key Components of Software CM

| Component | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Configuration Items (CIs)** | System/software assets requiring control (e.g., OS, hypervisor). Identified in the CM plan. |
| **Baselines** | Pre-configured CIs used as a consistent starting point. Tested, verified, then versioned (e.g., 1.1.2 → 1.1.3). |
| **Versions** | Uniquely identify functionality or baseline configuration. |
| **Change Sets** | Collective changes made to a baseline as part of a change request. |
| **Branches** | Configurations built alongside the baseline (a "build in progress"). Checking out a baseline creates a branch; checking it back in (after CCB approval) creates a new official baseline. |

### 3. The Change Management Process (3 Sub-processes)

| Sub-process | Function |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Request Control** | Procedures for *requesting* a change. |
| **Change Control** | Procedures for *identifying* the appropriate change (what's in the change set, which branch). |
| **Release Control** | Procedures for *deploying* the change to production/operations (pushing/rolling out). |

### 4. Step-by-Step Change Workflow
1. **Request** – Submit change to Change Control Board (CCB).
2. **Review** – Assess relevance, risk, impact.
3. **Build & Test** – Create proof of concept (still under change control).
4. **Approve/Reject** – CCB decides based on test results.
5. **Implement** – Push/roll out to production/ops (release control).
6. **Verify** – Check for negative impacts.
7. **Close Out** – Roll new baseline/version.

### 5. Key Benefits & Takeaways
- **Traceability & Accountability** – Multiple personnel involved at each step (requesters, testers, CCB, admins).
- **Governance** – If something fails, documentation allows rollback to previous baseline.
- **Bottom Line** – Understand the purpose of software CM and clearly understand the change management process.

### 1. Definition of Media  
- Any medium capable of storing data (HDD, SSD, tape, CD, DVD, mobile device, thumb drive, etc.).

### 2. Core Security Goal  
- Maintain **confidentiality, integrity, availability (CIA)** of data on media at all times.

### 3. Media Lifecycle & Availability  
- Media has a **finite lifespan** (mean time to failure).  
- Aging media can slow data retrieval → impacts **availability**.  
- Need **good inventory & asset tracking** to replace media before failure.

### 4. Relationship to Data Lifecycle  
- Media management focuses on the **storage phase** of the data lifecycle.  
- Data is created → labeled → stored on media → accessed → transferred to other media.

### 5. Marking & Labeling Assets (Critical)  
- **Physical marking** (e.g., “Secret” sticker on a hard drive) → identifies sensitivity/classification of data the media may contain.  
- **Digital labeling** (metadata, hard-coded) → ensures proper handling across systems.

### 6. Removable Media & Physical Controls  
- Use stickers, tags, markers.  
- **Encrypt** wherever possible.  
- Backup tapes → store in safes, lockable containers, vaults.  
- Media leaving facility → apply security controls for **transit/transport** protection.

### 7. Sanitization  
- When media is no longer needed → **properly sanitize** to prevent data remnant recovery.  
- Critical before reusing media at a lower classification level.

### 8. Proactive Replacement  
- Replace media before mean time to failure is realized.  
- Part of **continuous monitoring** and **asset security** to avoid availability loss or single points of failure.

### 9. Bottom Line  
- Understand the **purpose of media management**: protecting media throughout its lifecycle to uphold CIA.

Based on the transcript, here is a structural summary of the **Incident Management** process as presented, aligned with both the CISSP Common Body of Knowledge (CBK) and the NIST 800-61 framework.

### I. Core Definition
- **Incident:** An event (intentional or unintentional) that violates security policy.
- **Goal:** Manage, respond to, and recover from events that negatively impact the system.

### II. Key Frameworks (for reference)
- **Primary (Exam Focus):** NIST SP 800-61 (Rev 2) – *Computer Security Incident Handling Guide*.
- **Secondary:** ISO 27035, ISACA guides.

### III. The Incident Response Lifecycle (CISSP CBK Order)

#### 1. Detection
- **Sources:** System logs, IDS/IPS, endpoint security (firewalls), **personnel reports**.
- **Action:** Analyze events to verify if they constitute a security incident per policy.
- **Triage:** Determine severity and prioritize treatment (medical term adapted for security).

#### 2. Response
- **Trigger:** Based on severity level defined in the Incident Response Plan.
- **Team Activation:** CIRT (Computer Incident Response Team) or CSIRT.
- **Key Actions:**
    - Control damage/disruption.
    - Identify, collect, and handle evidence.
    - Thoroughly document everything.

#### 3. Mitigation
- **Purpose:** Quickly contain the incident to prevent further organizational impact.
- **Example:** Shutting down a port, isolating a network segment, blacklisting an IP.
- **Consideration:** Determine if Disaster Recovery (DR) or Business Continuity (BC) procedures are needed.

#### 4. Reporting
- **Timing:** After containment, not before (to avoid incomplete information).
- **Audiences:**
    - **Internal:** Senior management (status, impact, recovery timeline).
    - **External:** Required by regulations (e.g., GDPR mandates 72-hour breach notification).
- **Caution:** Exclude sensitive vulnerability/threat details from public reports.

#### 5. Recovering
- **Nature:** Temporary restoration to an operational state to prevent business impact.
- **Examples:** Re-enabling a network connection, restoring a system account, bringing a component back online.
- **Contingency:** If recovery exceeds MTD (Maximum Tolerable Downtime), activate BCP/DRP.

#### 6. Remediation
- **Nature:** Permanent restoration to full operational status.
- **Scope:** Address system damage, legal matters, financial impacts (e.g., investigation fees).

#### 7. Lessons Learned
- **Purpose:** Post-incident analysis to improve future response.
- **Key Questions:**
    - What happened and why?
    - What could have prevented it?
    - What can stakeholders do differently?
- **Output:** Update plans, controls, and monitor changes for effectiveness.

### IV. Foundational Preparations (Pre-Detection)
- **Policy:** Define objectives, scope, what constitutes an incident, priorities, KPIs/KRIs, and reporting requirements.
- **Resources:** Deploy tools (DLP, firewalls, storage), establish recovery sites.
- **Team:** Form a cohesive CIRT with appropriate skills (sysadmins, network, security, management).
- **Procedures:** Create step-by-step responses for possible scenarios; get buy-in from system owners and senior management.

Here is a structural summary of the video transcript on security investigations for the CSSP exam:

### 1. Core Purpose of an Investigation
- **Goal:** Collect and analyze facts about an event to reach a conclusion (determine if something did or did not happen).
- **Your Role:** Primarily a *support role* (collecting evidence, maintaining chain of custody, possibly testifying in court), unless you are a forensic investigator or the sole security professional.

### 2. Key Concepts & Terminology
- **Burden of Proof:** The obligation to prove the event took place (or didn't).
    - *Criminal proceeding:* Proof **beyond a reasonable doubt** (to a jury of peers).
    - *Civil proceeding:* **Preponderance of evidence** (majority/more likely than not).
- **Parties involved:**
    - *Criminal:* Plaintiff (accuser) vs. Defendant.
    - *Civil:* Claimant vs. Respondent.
- **Chain of Custody:** Must protect evidence and maintain an accurate record of who handled it and how.

### 3. Investigative Techniques
- **Interviewing:** Talking to personnel (admins, engineers, etc.) to gather information.
- **Interrogation:** A specific, more focused interview to determine if a subject committed a violation (usually for law enforcement, but usable in internal investigations).
- **Surveillance:** Monitoring a subject (e.g., via real-time logs, CCTV) to gather more evidence.
- **Digital Forensics:** Identifying, collecting, analyzing, and preserving electronic data from servers, workstations, endpoints, etc.

### 4. Types of Investigations (for the exam)
- **Administrative:** Violation of *organizational policy*.
- **Regulatory (Compliance):** Violation of a *law or regulation*.
- **Criminal:** Violation of *laws* (country/state level).
- **Civil:** Private or non-criminal matters (e.g., breach of contract, SLA, user agreement).

### 5. Investigative Mindset: *Modus Operandi* (Mode of Operations)
Focus on finding the root cause by examining three factors:
1.  **Motive:** Why did they do it?
2.  **Opportunity:** When and where could they do it?
3.  **Means:** Did they have the capability, tools, and techniques?

### 6. Exam Bottom Line
- The **accuser** (plaintiff/claimant) always has the burden of proof.
- Understand the different types of investigations at a high level (not how to execute them in detail).

Here’s a **structural summary** of the video on *Evidence Collection and Handling* for the CISSP exam:

---

## 1. Purpose of Evidence
- **Definition**: Facts/data proving an incident occurred.
- **Goal**: Demonstrate a security incident occurred; prove/disprove root cause.
- **Admissibility**: Evidence must be directly relevant to the incident; judge decides admissibility based on laws/regulations.

---

## 2. Types of Evidence

| Type | Description | Examples |
|------|-------------|----------|
| **Real** | Tangible objects | Fingerprints on keyboard, video recording, screen scrape |
| **Documentary** | Written proof of facts/statements | Audit logs, entry/exit logs (must be authenticated) |
| **Testimonial** | Written/verbal witness statements | Witness describing what they saw |
| **Demonstrative** (corroborating) | Helps demonstrate testimony | Diagrams, models, supporting evidence |
| **Direct** | Witness directly observed the offense | Saw attacker typing commands |
| **Hearsay** | Secondhand knowledge (“someone told me”) | “John told me he saw the attacker” |
| **Opinion** | Expert statement | Forensic analyst explaining attack method |
| **Circumstantial** | Facts combined to infer offense | Multiple indirect clues pointing to guilt |
| **Corroborative** | Supports/validates a claim | Video + logs matching hearsay statement |

---

## 3. Key Legal Rules

- **Best Evidence Rule**: Use **original** documentation whenever possible; copies are **secondary evidence** (less admissible, harder to authenticate).
- **Parol Evidence Rule**: Verbal agreements about evidence must be put **in writing** to become documentary evidence.

---

## 4. Chain of Custody (Critical)
- **Definition**: Proper handling, marking, tracking of each piece of evidence.
- **Why vital**: Breaks in chain introduce doubt → evidence may be thrown out.
- **Document** for every transfer:
  - What was transferred (hard drive, logs, etc.)
  - Who transferred to whom
  - When (date/time to seconds)
  - How (physical, digital, envelope, etc.)
  - Signatures of **both parties** for custody change

---

## 5. Collection Best Practices
- Get a **second opinion** / second person present during witness interviews.
- Avoid **investigator bias** (don’t try to prove a preconceived narrative).
- **Document everything**: IP addresses, nodes, rooms, buildings—nothing is overkill.

---

## 6. Example Scenario (Insider Threat)
- **Real**: Thumb drive, video footage  
- **Documentary**: Audit logs  
- **Testimonial/Direct**: Sysadmin witnessed act  
- **Hearsay**: Coworker heard argument but didn’t see  
- **Opinion**: External web admin forensic analysis  
- **Circumstantial**: Employee saw insider in data center  
- **Corroborative**: Access logs + video of entry

---

## 7. Bottom Line for CISSP
- Know the **different types of evidence**.
- Understand the **purpose and mechanics of chain of custody**.
- Apply **best evidence rule** and **parol evidence rule** appropriately.

| **RPO** (Recovery Point Objective) | Acceptable data loss (measured in time, backups, baselines) |

Here’s a **structured summary** of the video transcript on *Disaster Recovery Strategies*:

---

## 1. Core Concepts
- **Disaster**: Event causing major damage/destruction (facility, resources, property, or life).
- **Business Continuity**: Focuses on **critical business functions**.
- **Disaster Recovery**: Focuses on **assets supporting those functions**.

---

## 2. Key Recovery Strategies

| Strategy | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| **System Resilience** | System’s ability to recover from disruption; minimizes single points of failure. |
| **Fault Tolerance** | System continues operating *during* a failure (built into system). |
| **High Availability** | Uses redundant systems (servers, apps) for quick recovery over long periods. |

> Resilience is the umbrella term; fault tolerance & HA are sub-types.

---

## 3. Data Protection: RAID Levels

| RAID Level | Name | Fault Tolerance | Description |
|------------|------|----------------|-------------|
| RAID‑0 | Striping | ❌ No | Data split across disks; performance only. |
| RAID‑1 | Mirroring | ✅ Yes | Identical copies on 2 disks; resource‑intensive. |
| RAID‑5 | Striping with parity | ✅ Yes | 3+ disks, one for parity; slower if a disk fails. |
| RAID‑10 | Stripe of mirrors | ✅ Yes | 4+ disks; combines striping & mirroring. |

---

## 4. Server & Network Resilience

- **Failover Cluster**: Multiple servers/nodes share workload; if one fails, others take over.
- **Load Balancing**: Distributes traffic/processes across servers (via load balancer or cluster).

---

## 5. Power Protection

| Solution | Duration | Notes |
|----------|----------|-------|
| **UPS** (uninterruptible power supply) | Short period | Battery or flywheel; needs space inside data center. |
| **Generator** | Long period | Motor‑driven; needs fuel & maintenance. |

**Additional**: Voltage regulators, line conditioners, surge protectors.

---

## 6. Network Communications: QoS
**Quality of Service (QoS)** prioritizes critical traffic on limited‑capacity networks.  
Handles: throughput, bandwidth, latency, jitter, errors.  
Requires: traffic identification → classification → device configuration.

---

## 7. Failure States (Critical for Firewalls & Network Devices)

| State | Behavior |
|-------|----------|
| **Fail open** | Defaults to allowing all access during failure (insecure). |
| **Fail safe / fail secure** | Defaults to allowing nothing; system stays secure. |

> Always design devices to **fail in a secure state** (closed).

---

## 8. Integrated Example (from diagram description)
- Redundant switches, servers, load balancers → failover / HA.
- RAID for storage redundancy.
- UPS or generator for power outages.
- QoS for traffic prioritization under stress.

---

## 9. Bottom Line (Exam Takeaways)
- Know recovery methods (resilience, fault tolerance, HA).
- Know protection methods (RAID, failover clusters, power protection).
- Understand QoS and failure states (fail safe vs. fail open).

Here’s a structural summary of the video transcript on **disaster recovery sites** for the CISSP exam:

---

## 1. Purpose of a Recovery Site (Alternate Processing Site)
- Used temporarily after a disaster or major disruption at the primary site.
- Focuses on **IT assets** (networks, servers, databases, etc.) supporting business functions.
- Not for permanent relocation; typical duration = days (depends on disaster severity and stakeholder-defined tolerances).

---

## 2. Selection Criteria
- Based on **Business Impact Analysis (BIA)** results, especially **Maximum Tolerable Downtime (MTD)**.
- Also considers **Recovery Time Objective (RTO)** and budget.

---

## 3. Types of Recovery Sites

| Site Type | Infrastructure / Equipment | Data | Cost | Activation Time |
|-----------|---------------------------|------|------|----------------|
| **Cold Site** | Empty room/warehouse; no computing equipment | None | Lowest | Days to weeks |
| **Warm Site** | Pre-configured computing equipment, basic infrastructure (HVAC, electricity, patch/baseline servers) | No operational data (only system data) | Moderate | ~12 hours |
| **Hot Site** | Full suite: computers, networks, near-real-time data, full infrastructure | Near real-time (copied daily/hourly) | Very high | Minutes to a few hours |

---

## 4. Other Recovery Options

- **Mobile Site**  
  - Self-contained, transportable (shipping container, tractor-trailer).  
  - Typically configured as **cold or warm** site.  
  - Contains critical assets; can be moved geographically.

- **Cloud-Managed Recovery Site**  
  - Hosted on AWS, Azure, GCP, etc.  
  - Usually **warm or hot**.  
  - Key: **SLA** defines roles, availability, performance, data rates, costs (metered by VM uptime).

- **Shared Site**  
  - Shared with one or more external organizations.  
  - Governed by **Mutual Assistance Agreement (MAA)** or reciprocal agreement.  
  - Rare due to data sensitivity and legal issues.

---

## 5. Critical Requirement
- **Geographic isolation** from the primary site (e.g., different city/region) to avoid the same disaster impacting both sites.

---

## 6. Exam Takeaway
- Know **purpose** of recovery sites.  
- Understand **what is present** at cold, warm, hot, mobile, cloud, and shared sites.  
- Activation time and cost are inversely related to readiness.

## 1. Core Purpose of Backup
- Duplicate data to retrieve it later after data loss or system failure.
- Critical for disaster recovery (DR).

## 2. Key Concepts
- **Mirroring**: Identical copy on ≥2 storage media (e.g., RAID).
- **Archive bit (backup bit)**:  
  - `0` = backed up (no change since last backup).  
  - `1` = needs backup (file changed).

## 3. Backup Types

| Type | What it does | Archive bit after backup |
|------|--------------|--------------------------|
| **Full** | Complete copy of all data | Sets all to `0` |
| **Differential** | Changes since **last full backup** | Does not reset (leaves `1`) |
| **Incremental** | Changes since **any last backup** (full/diff/inc) | Resets to `0` |

- **Full**: large, infrequent (e.g., Sundays).
- **Differential**: medium, captures everything since last full.
- **Incremental**: small, frequent (e.g., daily except full/diff days).

## 4. 3-2-1 Backup Rule
- **3** copies of data.
- **2** different devices/media on-premise.
- **1** copy off-premise.

## 5. Off-Premise Backup (Electronic Vaulting)
- **Remote journaling**: logs + metadata off-site (for audit/analysis).
- **Remote mirroring**: real-time streaming of changes off-site.
- Recovery needs both **journal** + backup data.

## 6. Storage Media
- Disks, tapes, external drives — no mandated method (org chooses).

## 7. Snapshots
- Virtual copies of files, dirs, volumes, VMs (e.g., via hypervisor).

## 8. Escrow Arrangements
- **Key/certificate escrow**: third-party agent stores crypto keys; recovery agent accesses.
- **Software escrow**: stores source code, licenses, docs — protects if vendor fails.

## 9. Rotation Schedules (historical exam topics)
- FIFO, Grandfather-Father-Son, Tower of Hanoi.
- Key point: ensure chosen schedule meets **compliance retention requirements** (1, 3, 5, 10 years, etc.).

## 10. Exam Takeaway
Know:
- Backup types (full, diff, inc) + archive bit behavior.
- Electronic vaulting methods.
- Escrow arrangements (key/cert, software).

Based on the video transcript, here is a structured summary of the **disaster recovery processes**:

### 1. Core Focus & Definition
- **Goal:** Ensure critical business assets and processes (IT infrastructure: servers, workstations, databases, websites) remain operational after a disruption.
- **Scope:** Applies to on-premise, off-premise (remote/cloud), local, or remote assets.
- **Reference Standard:** NIST SP 800-34 (Contingency Planning Guide).

### 2. Priority Hierarchy
1.  **Human Life (Top Priority):** Safety and security of personnel overrides all technology concerns.
2.  **Communication:** Essential for assessing safety and coordinating response.
3.  **Technology Recovery:** Only after human safety is addressed.

### 3. Key Processes within the DRP

| Process | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Documentation** | Assign a scribe/spokesperson as single point of contact for clear, consistent communication with management, emergency services, and media. |
| **Training & Awareness** | Ensure team members know roles, responsibilities, first aid, fire suppression, crisis management, evidence collection, and collaboration with law enforcement/emergency services. |
| **Response** | Define procedures based on disaster type (natural or manmade). Activate the **Business Continuity Plan (BCP)** if Recovery Time Objective (RTO) or Recovery Point Objective (RPO) cannot be met. |
| **Personnel** | Define roles, responsibilities, response times, and **primary/alternate (backup)** personnel for each role to account for absence due to the disaster. |
| **Communications** | Use a single recognizable voice to relay activation status, situation updates, and instructions internally and externally (media, law enforcement). Maintain a contact information table. |
| **Assessment** | Investigate disruption extent, impact on tolerance levels (RTO/RPO), sales, reputation, contracts, legal/regulatory compliance, and risk to human life. Triage the situation. |
| **Restoration** | Move operations back to the **original primary location** (vs. recovery = bringing systems back to normal at any site). Restore **least critical functions first** to avoid impacting critical operations if a failure recurs. |
| **Lessons Learned** | Evaluate personnel performance, team speed, tolerance impacts, communication effectiveness. Identify what went right/wrong and corrective actions for future prevention, detection, and response. |

### 4. Key Exam Takeaways
- **BCP vs. DRP:** BCP identifies critical business functions and drives the overall plan; DRP is a subset focused on **recovering the technology infrastructure** that supports those functions.
- **Top Priority:** Always choose human life first in any exam question.
- **Recovery vs. Restoration:**
    - *Recovery* = bringing systems back to normal condition (possibly at alternate site).
    - *Restoration* = returning systems to original state at primary location.

Here is a structural summary of the video transcript on the Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC) for the CISSP exam.

### 1. Core Concept
- **Definition:** A series of phases moving software from inception to retirement (creation to recreation).
- **Goal:** Increase software maturity through iterative phases.
- **Exam Focus:** Based on **NIST SP 800-64** (System Development Lifecycle), though withdrawn in 2019.
- **Newer Standard:** NIST SP 800-160 (System Security Engineering) – maps similarly to the old phases.

### 2. The Five Phases (NIST SP 800-64)

| Phase | Key Activities |
| :--- | :--- |
| **1. Initiation** | Define need, purpose, requirements, organizational objectives. Identify privacy/data protection needs. Decide build vs. buy. Conduct Privacy Impact Assessment (PIA) & business impact assessment. |
| **2. Development & Acquisition** | Assess risks (especially for third-party/COTS products). Determine initial security & privacy controls. Create/update security documentation & architecture design. Perform risk analysis. |
| **3. Implementation** | Obtain stakeholder approval. Securely deploy to operations/production. Conduct security assessment/audit for compliance. Integrate security into the environment. |
| **4. Operations & Maintenance (O&M)** | Provide designed functionality. Apply configuration management & change control (CCB). Continuously monitor security control effectiveness. Adapt controls to new threats/vulnerabilities. |
| **5. Disposal** | Remove from operations. Sanitize/declassify software and data. Apply CM and change control during removal. Preserve records for audit. Dispose of hardware/software. |

### 3. Key Cross-Cutting Principles
- **Documentation:** Must be continuously updated as changes occur.
- **Risk & Privacy:** Assessed from initiation through disposal.
- **Change Control:** Critical from O&M phase onward, but also during disposal.
- **Continuous Monitoring:** Applies especially in O&M and disposal phases.

### 4. Exam Bottom Line
- **Must know:** Each phase and its specific activities.
- **Note:** Even though NIST SP 800-64 is withdrawn, exam questions will still refer to it.

Here is a structural summary of the video transcript:

## 1. Introduction
- Two-part series on software development methodologies.
- Follows the SDLC (Software Development Lifecycle).
- This video covers selected methodologies; next video covers the rest.

## 2. Waterfall Model
- **Origin**: Created by Winston Royce in 1970.
- **Nature**: Sequential, repetitive (iterative), feedback loops allowed.
- **Core phases** (exam-relevant):
  1. Requirements (system/software)
  2. Design (preliminary/detailed)
  3. Implementation (coding & debugging)
  4. Testing
  5. Operations & maintenance
- **Drawbacks**:
  - All requirements must be known upfront.
  - Structured process limits flexibility and agility.
  - No disposal/retirement phase.
- **Best for**: Sensitive, high-risk, or methodical applications.

## 3. Incremental Build Model
- **Concept**: Build software in smaller, achievable chunks (increments).
- **Process per increment**:
  1. Analysis / requirements
  2. Design
  3. Coding
  4. Testing
  5. Delivery
- **Key traits**:
  - System engineering done upfront during analysis & design.
  - Each increment informs the next (lessons learned, adaptation).
  - Predates but resembles agile.

## 4. Spiral Model
- **Approach**: Product revisits development phases multiple times.
- **Typical steps per loop**:
  - Planning
  - Risk analysis (software development risk, not security risk)
  - Engineering
  - Evaluation
- **Visual concept**: Multiple prototypes moving through phases, allowing backward fixes and rework.
- **Drawback**: Difficult to build security into the process due to parallel/iterative tracking.

## 5. Key Takeaways for Exam
- Know each step of the **waterfall model**.
- Understand the **purpose** of the incremental build model.
- Understand the **purpose** of the spiral model.
- Security integration is better addressed in other methodologies (next video).

## 1. Cleanroom Reference Model (CRM)
- **Focus:** Defect prevention via rigorous engineering & quality control.
- **Origin:** Carnegie Mellon University / Software Engineering Institute.
- **Named after:** Hardware cleanrooms (strict procedures).
- **Four principle functions:**  
  1. Software management  
  2. Specification  
  3. Development  
  4. Certification  
- **Process:** 14 processes → 20 work products (guides, plans, cases) to prove software is defect-free.

---

## 2. Joint Application Development (JAD)
- **Focus:** Continuous interaction between user and developer.
- **Goals:** Reduce timeframes, cost, and improve quality via direct feedback.
- **Process (JAD sessions):**  
  1. Define objectives (requirements, scope, stakeholders)  
  2. Session preparation (gather info)  
  3. Session conduct (fix issues)  
  4. Documentation (publish for review)

---

## 3. Rapid Application Development (RAD)
- **Origin:** Response to Waterfall’s rigidity.
- **Focus:** Working software over strict project management.
- **Often combined with:** JAD + CASE tools.
- **Best for:** Prototypes, R&D, proof of concept, minimum viable product.
- **Steps:**  
  1. Requirements (scope, outcomes)  
  2. User design (gather expectations)  
  3. Construction (develop, update, test)  
  4. Cutover (deliver to customer/operations)

---

## 4. Quick Selection Guide (from the video)

| Methodology | Best for |
|-------------|----------|
| **Waterfall** | Methodical approach with known requirements, critical applications, sensitive data |
| **Spiral** | Responding quickly to changes/risks in large/complex projects |
| **Incremental Build** | Faster Waterfall with flexibility for scope changes & user feedback |
| **Cleanroom** | Formal, strict defect prevention |
| **JAD** | Constant user input & satisfaction, short timelines |
| **RAD** | Fast development/deployment/feedback, R&D, proof of concept |

## 1. **DevOps Basics**
- **Definition**: Combines **development** and **operations** (people, processes, technology) to rapidly develop and deliver software.
- **Goal**: Enable **agile development** → frequent delivery of **minimum viable product** (MVP), then iterative refinement.
- **High‑level cycle**: Plan → Develop → Deliver → Operate → (back to Plan).  
  Core themes: collaboration, workflow, **security & compliance**.

---

## 2. **DevOps Workflow / Pipeline**
- **Pipeline** = automated workflow for continuous integration & delivery (CI/CD).
- Includes: development, QA/QC, security testing, software testing.
- **Challenge**: Maintaining **separation of duties** (hard due to integrated roles).
- **Infrastructure as Code (IaC)**:
  - Provision infra (networks, VMs, load balancers) via code (XML, Python, tools like Chef, Ansible, Terraform).
  - Increases speed, consistency; reduces risk & cost.
  - **Immutable architecture** = static, trusted, fully CM‑controlled.

---

## 3. **Security & Role Management in DevOps**
- **Key principles**: Separation of duties, **least privilege**.
- Risk: **Privilege/authorization creep** – especially with automation tools (e.g., Jenkins).
- Must enforce RBAC across developers, security engineers, analysts.

---

## 4. **DevSecOps** (Development + Security + Operations)
- **Also called**: Security as Code (built into pipeline).
- **Mindset shift** (DevSecOps Manifesto – summary of principles):
  - Lean in / solve problems (vs. just saying “no”).
  - Data & science over fear/uncertainty/doubt.
  - Open collaboration, consumable security APIs, business‑driven scores.
  - Red/blue team testing over theoretical scans.
  - 24/7 proactive monitoring, shared threat intel, compliance **operations** (not checklists).

- **Exam takeaway**: DevSecOps = proactive, solution‑focused security, not rigid doctrine.

---

## 5. **CI/CD** (Continuous Integration / Continuous Delivery)
- **Continuous Integration**: Automates integrating new code into existing codebase.
- **Continuous Delivery**: Automates delivering the integrated codebase.
- **Continuous Deployment**: Automated delivery to **end users** (final pipeline step).
- **Pipeline flow example**:  
  Build → Test (unit) → Deploy to test env → Automated checks/scans → Deploy to production → Assess/monitor → Update version → Repeat.

---

## 6. **Where Security Fits in the Pipeline** (baked in, not bolted on)
- **Version control** → Be on change control board.
- **Build** → Build in controls & requirements.
- **Testing** → Compliance checks.
- **Test environment** → Security audits, compliance tests, vulnerability scans.
- **Production deployment** → Security regression testing.
- **Operations & maintenance** → Continuous monitoring (patches, threats, vulnerabilities).

---

## 7. **Benefits of CI/CD Pipelines**
- Faster, **consistent deliveries** (with proper security as code).
- Faster customer feedback on performance/functionality.
- Rapid response to discovered vulnerabilities (add mitigation → roll new version through pipeline).
- Faster & consistent application of security to codebases.

---

## 8. **Bottom Line for Exam**
- Purpose & benefits of **DevOps** and **DevSecOps**.
- Purpose of **Infrastructure as Code** & **Security as Code**.
- Purpose & benefits of **CI/CD**.

```Welcome to this video on software operations and maintenance. As part of the CISSP exam, you are expected to understand operations and maintenance as it pertains to the software development lifecycle. Operations and maintenance is pretty straightforward. It's just making sure that the software application securely provides its intended function or purpose. And what we mean by operations and maintenance, or O&M, is when the software has been deployed, it's now running in production, or it's in an operations environment, and now we need to make sure that it stays up and running and stays secure. So what we have to do is focus on ensuring that the software remains operational and prevents any kind of compromise to confidentiality, integrity, or availability. The main way that we do that is through software patch management. So once the software application's in operations, typically there are going to be flaws. There are going to be things wrong with it, and eventually it's going to need to be patched, and it must be part of an overall patch management policy to address those flaws or those bugs in those software applications. We should also follow a strict and consistent process for identifying and installing these patches or fix actions. The reason this is important to be consistent is because the software application is in CRUD, or it's in OPs, so it's running, customers are using it, and the organization is depending upon it. And this is very important to know for the CISSP exam. So the patch management process you should be familiar with all starts with evaluation. We want to identify patches and determine the risk to the system. The risk to the system is going to determine how important this patch is. So if we just get a common patch, maybe it's just a simple web browser patch or something like that. If it's not a web browser that affects us, let's say a patch comes out for Mozilla Firefox, but we don't use Firefox, then that patch is irrelevant; the risk is non-existent. But if we use Google Chrome, or we use Microsoft Edge, or something else, if we're using those and those have a patch, now we need to identify what does that patch solve? Does that patch solve a security risk? Does it solve a functionality problem? Is it because it added new fonts or because it added some new feature? That's not really a security risk or an operational risk, but if there's a cross-site scripting vulnerability, that increases the security risk rapidly. So that means that we need to pay attention to this patch. It becomes a critical install at this point, and now we need to go ahead and move it to test. So now we want to evaluate this patch in a test environment in some way to look for any kind of negative impacts. So when we install this patch, does the browser stop working? Does a certain feature get disabled? Does it change the security control baseline? What happens when we install this patch? If there's no negative impacts, then it's not a big deal. Then we move to the approval process where we take it to the stakeholders, and typically this is going to be done as part of configuration management. We would take this to the change control board. We would ask for authorization to install, the subject matter experts would take a look at it, and once the CCB approves this, now we would move into rollout or deployment in this case. We would roll the patch out, install it on all the production hosts that are necessary, and then once that's done, we want to verify that everything has been installed, it's working properly, and we also want to verify that nothing has regressed in terms of security, and we want to move through this process as fast and as efficiently as possible. So this needs to be laid out as part of the configuration management plan. Now, as part of step five of this process, I mentioned regression. What is regression? Software can regress, meaning, a patch or a bug fix can cause unwanted changes, regress the configuration, or regress the security baseline in the software application. And it could be based on the vendor's fix action, it could be based on a configuration setting and so on. As part of that verification process, we want to perform regression testing to make sure that whenever we install the patch, that it doesn't open up new attack vectors, that it doesn't create new vulnerabilities, that we don't have new threats. Now, because of this patch, and if you've ever patched a system before, you know, sometimes patches can cause unwanted damage. You can install a patch, it reconfigures the system, and now the system's not working like it once did. Or there might be a bug fix, and in that bug fix, there's a feature configuration change, and now all of a sudden you have new features, and now you have to research those to determine, "Hey, are these security relevant?" And that's why we performed that testing. That early testing in step two, we would test it and determine what would happen, and that hopefully eliminates the possibility of a regression happening in the system. Now, there's a variety of regression tests that we can perform as part of this verification. We can perform a unit test where we look at individual functionality. If we patch something that was focused on the individual functionality, we would target the source code if possible, to determine if that software is ready or not to continue operations, or it's ready to go ahead and be verified and accept it. We can perform a functional test where we're ensuring that the software meets operational requirements. Now, once we've made that patch update, does the system still meet the functional requirements or the operational requirements that we have set forth? If not, then we need to roll the patch back, because that baseline was approved by the change control board under the configuration management process. We can also perform an integration test, which makes sure that the software is still interacting properly between different technologies, and then once we patch it, maybe something breaks, maybe a new API feature comes in, and then that breaks the API connection because the keys need to be reinstalled. But an integration test would help us discover that. And then obviously we can do a security test where we verify that the software meets security requirements. Now, by far and away, this is probably the most common regression test that we will do, is we will verify either we'll do a vulnerability assessment and maybe we just do a quick security assessment to check various controls. It really depends on your organization and also your compliance requirements. But in this case, we would test it, make sure that it still meets the security requirements, and then go ahead and approve that change. Now, one of the most efficient ways to do this is to implement this via DevOps. So to create a CICD, continuous integration, continuous delivery pipeline, and that way we're checking everything throughout the entire process. So if you recall back to the DevOps and the DevSecOps video where we talked about infrastructure as code, security as code, those kinds of things, this is when we would build that in. So in this case, we have our version, which is our current baseline. Then once the patch has been identified and been evaluated and we know we need it, then what we would do is we would move it into Build where we installed that patch onto whatever host, and that would be within a test environment. So then we would do a unit test or whatever we would do here. If we have separate test environments or integration environments, we can move them along in this path. And then we can automate the test right here. Maybe we want to do an automated security test, maybe a security scan, a vulnerability scan, something like that. Or what if we have some kind of a SCAP scan where we're doing a control scan to make sure that everything is set correct and nothing regressed. And then at that point we go ahead and get the approval to move it to production, and then at that point we go ahead and validate or verify that everything's in place, and then we roll the new version. So we can do that as part of DevOps, and that's highly recommended, because it's a consistent process. Now again, make sure to incorporate operations and maintenance processes into the configuration management plan. It should be part of the configuration management process, so it has to be in the plan. And we want to evaluate the performance of O&M as part of continuous monitoring. So we're not making any of the changes. Part of the maintenance part of it is just making sure that our security baseline remains intact. So we're doing those periodic assessments, those periodic tests, to make sure things are solid. That way we're not getting rogue patches installed, we're not getting rogue bug fixes installed and things like that. That might also help us identify maybe there's some back doors where there's an automatic update installed where there shouldn't be, and we're getting patches from the outside. This will help with all of that. So the bottom line for O&M is to understand the purpose of software O&M, know about regressions and regression testing, and also know that O&M must be part of the CM plan.```

Here is a structural summary of the video transcript on **Software Operations and Maintenance (O&M)** for the CISSP exam:

### 1. Definition & Purpose of O&M
- **What it is:** Ensuring a software application securely provides its intended function after deployment in a production environment.
- **Primary goal:** Keep the software operational while preventing compromises to **confidentiality, integrity, and availability (CIA)**.

### 2. Core Activity: Patch Management
- **Why needed:** Software flaws/bugs will inevitably arise post-deployment.
- **Key principle:** Follow a strict, consistent process (integrated into the configuration management plan).

### 3. The 5-Step Patch Management Process
1.  **Evaluation:** Identify patches and assess risk to the system (critical vs. irrelevant).
2.  **Test:** Evaluate the patch in a test environment for negative impacts (e.g., broken features, changed security baselines).
3.  **Approval:** Present to the Change Control Board (CCB) as part of configuration management.
4.  **Rollout/Deployment:** Install the patch on production hosts.
5.  **Verification:** Confirm correct installation, proper functioning, and **no regressions**.

### 4. Key Concept: Regression & Regression Testing
- **Regression:** Unwanted changes caused by a patch (new vulnerabilities, broken functionality, altered security baseline).
- **Types of regression tests:**
    - **Unit test:** Individual functionality.
    - **Functional test:** Operational requirements.
    - **Integration test:** Interactions between technologies.
    - **Security test:** Security requirements (most common, includes vulnerability assessments).

### 5. Recommended Implementation: DevOps / CI/CD Pipeline
- Integrate O&M into a **CI/CD pipeline**.
- Automate testing (security scans, vulnerability scans, SCAP scans) within the pipeline.
- Move through: **Baseline → Build (test) → Approve → Production → Validate**.

### 6. Final Takeaways for CISSP Exam
- **O&M must be part of the Configuration Management (CM) Plan.**
- Evaluate O&M performance as part of **continuous monitoring** (periodic assessments to ensure security baseline remains intact).
- Understand the purpose of O&M, regressions/regression testing, and the CM plan integration.

```Welcome to this video on Integrated Product Teams. In this case or in this conversation, it's a software product. And then within the approach for development, you'll see teams, and you'll see this in a Venn diagram, which means everything is intersecting. And that's the idea, that we're integrating the tools, the teams, and the development process, all within a disciplined approach to create this product on behalf of the customer. And that's exactly what we're trying to do. Within the realm of what we do, we could have developers, IT personnel like system administrators or network administrators. We can have project managers, we can have architects, certainly security were going to be involved, engineers, you name it. Anyone and everyone could be part of the integrated product team. There can also be third-party auditors, quality assurance or quality control staff, senior management, senior stakeholders. There could be a lot of different people embedded into this integrated product team. And if you recall back to the Agile Development video, I talked about a project manager being a Scrum Master. So this could be your Scrum Master. And again, you have the development team here, and then you have other folks that are all part of those teams. The idea here is that we're all going to have to work together at some level to get this product built and delivered to this customer. So the benefits of a good, solid IPT is that you're reducing time and cost to deliver an operational product. And this is because of the diverse skill sets that are part of the IPT. If you only have one individual, a manager is not going to know how to do security, and a security person is not going to know how to do management in some cases. Same with system administration. They won't know how to do engineering, but they'll know how to do administration. But when we bring everybody together, that will help us reduce operational security risk upfront, because we're going to have good solid planning with our subject matter expertise and also good solid engineering as part of this process. And then the IPT will result in better quality with continuous improvement involved as well. Now, within the IPT, there are some priorities. The customer focus is the top priority. This is going to determine the outcome of the project, what processes we're going to use, and also the schedule we're looking at in terms of how fast we need to develop this product. And we also want to be proactive with our risk management. That's both for the product and security, and we want to use tools that do not interfere with the development process. So that's why we call them seamless. We want them to be unseen, we don't want them to affect the outcome of delivery. That means while we're doing, say, a risk analysis or risk assessment, we don't want to impact what the other IPT team members are working on at this current time. We want to do our work while they do their work and then bring everything together. So in terms of risk, we're talking cost, schedule, technical impacts. All of those should be considered as part of risk as it pertains to the product we're developing. We should also concurrently develop products and processes to improve the overall lifecycle. So as we're going through the development process, we should be identifying places that we can improve: lessons learned, maybe this process didn't work correctly, maybe this technique is no longer valid, maybe this tool that we're using is no longer effective. Quality control has a different point of view. So, it's critical that these processes that we use to manage the process are effective in how we develop, how we build, how we verify, test, deploy, and so on. ```Welcome to this video on code repositories. On the CISSP exam, you may see a question about code repositories, so we need to cover that here in this video. Now, a code repository, or a code repo as it's called, is a centralized storage location for software code. So we use repos to store our software code for a variety of reasons. It can provide web hosting, it can provide notifications, wiki pages, and more to support collaborative software development. So we can host certain pages where we talk about the different code. We can have notifications when people check code in and out. Maybe they check out a new branch from a baseline, something like that. We will get notifications via email and also console notifications as well. There are wiki pages just in case you want to create something in terms of a user guide or something like that, and a lot of other things that can help us collaborate when we're building software. And naturally, it can provide secure storage, it can provide code review, version control, flaw and bug tracking, and more. There's a lot that you can do with these repos. Now, Git is the most commonly used language for tracking changes for software code files. So you might heard of GitHub. There's GitLab. There's a lot of different versions of Git and how it's implemented. Now, Git was developed by Linus Torvalds. This is the creator of Linux or Linux as it's called. This was released in 2005 and is since maintained by a lot of other individuals. Git will allow developers to interact with software files, create, modify, and remove files in these different repos. So it supports tracking of the file changes, and that's how we track version control within these repos. And again, some popular repos you might've heard of are GitHub, GitLab, there's SourceForge, there's Bitbucket, ProjectLocker, there's CodeCommit, Azure repos. There's so many different repos that are out there that we can use, and a majority of them use the Git language to manage the repository. And here's an example of how this repo might work. Let's say we have three different development teams and they're working out of a single repository. So let's say we have a GitHub account and we have a repo in GitHub. You can also do a git clone, which checks out a repo so you can work with it, similar to what we do with branch control. So as you can imagine, there's a lot of data moving to and from this repo. So how do we enforce security on the repo itself or for the repo? | **Level 1** | Low assurance (bare minimum) | Low-effort threats, easy-to-exploit vulnerabilities, script kiddies | First step in multi-phase effort; basic security. |
| **Level 2** | Moderate assurance | Skilled & motivated hackers, most penetration testing | Most applications needing robust defenses. |
| **Level 3** | High assurance | Advanced threats (e.g., APT - Advanced Persistent Threat) | Applications whose compromise would severely impact operations. |

### 4. Criteria for Determining Assurance Levels (Evaluation Criteria)
- **Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC):** Effective built-in security process.
- **Risk Analysis:** All risks must be known and accepted. Unacceptable/unmitigable risks cap level at 1.
- **Change Control:** Tightly controlled, authorized by a change control board.
- **Continuous Monitoring:** Ensuring controls remain effective & compliant over time (includes SAST/DAST assessments).
- **Data Protection:** Compliance with regulations (GDPR, SOX, HIPAA, etc.).
- **Logging:** Transactions and changes on the software and change control process.

### 5. Bottom Line for Exam
- Know the different **ASVS levels** (1, 2, 3).
- Understand the **evaluation criteria** of controls for each level.

---

## 1. Definition of Acquired Software
- Purchased or leased from a third party → organization has **no security control** over development.
- Examples:
  - **COTS** (Commercial Off-the-Shelf) – purchased/leased, organization manages installation, patching, etc.
  - **OSS / FOSS** (Open Source / Free Open Source Software) – no purchase, but acquired (e.g., GitHub, SourceForge).

  - **NDI** (Non-Developmental Items) – third-party libraries/modules included in COTS/GOTS/OSS → introduces **supply chain risk**.

## 2. Leased Software in the Cloud
- **SaaS** (Software as a Service) – provider owns OS & supporting apps; organization controls only **data & access controls**.
- **PaaS** (Platform as a Service) – provider owns OS; organization may own the application (but possibly no source code access).
- Security impacts: patching, upgrades, OS vulnerabilities, end-of-life concerns.

---

## 3. Key Security Strategy for Acquired Software
- Define an **acquisition policy/process** to minimize security risk.
- **Understand threats/vulnerabilities** specific to the acquired application.

---

## 4. Supply Chain Risk Management
- Investigate trusted vendors/suppliers/providers.
- Research track record, past violations, request documentation.
- Define **security responsibilities & SLAs** for cloud-based apps.
- For SaaS: understand how data is collected, used, transmitted, stored.

---

## 5. Acquisition Controls (per NIST SP 800-160 / 800-64)
1. **Preparation** – define security requirements in product/service request.
2. **Advertise & select supplier** – choose based on security criteria.
3. **Establish security aspects of agreement** – SLA/contract, evaluate changes.
4. **Monitor agreement** – assess execution against SLA.
5. **Accept product/service** – confirm compliance before purchase/license.

---

## 6. Operational Best Practices
- Implement access controls to prevent unauthorized app installation.
- Follow vendor/industry hardening guides for COTS/GOTS/OSS.
- **Test all acquired products** for vulnerabilities before production.
- Monitor acquired apps for **new threats and vulnerabilities** over time.

---

## 7. Bottom Line (Exam Takeaway)
- Understand risks of acquired applications.
- Define and follow a good acquisition policy/procedure.
- Doing so **reduces security risks** of acquired software.

Here is a structural summary of the video transcript on **Application Attacks**:

### 1. Definition & General Scope
- **Target:** Source-level code flaws.
- **Focus Areas:** Inputs, session management, process operations.
- **Entry Point:** Typically through the user interface of the application.

### 2. Types of Application Attacks

**A. Injection Attacks**
- **Concept:** Submitting unauthorized queries/code to a backend system via the app interface.
- **Varieties:**
    - *SQL Injection:* Unauthorized queries to a database.
    - *LDAP Injection:* Unauthorized queries to a directory server (e.g., Active Directory).
    - *XML Injection:* Unauthorized queries to an XML-based application.
    - *DLL Injection:* Placing malicious code in a Microsoft-specific DLL file.
- **Defenses:** Constrained interfaces, access control, input validation, hardening servers.

**B. Hijacking Attacks**
- **Session Hijack:** Assuming an authorized user’s active session by reusing session tokens, cookies, or credentials (also called replay attack).
- **Domain Hijack:** Unauthorized changes to a registered domain name (e.g., modifying DNS records).

**C. Backdoor Attacks**
- **Definition:** Bypassing normal authentication.
- **Common Causes:**
    - Developers embedding backdoors for maintenance (then forgotten in production).
    - Hard-coding authentication credentials into source code.
- **Defense:** Source code analysis before deployment.

**D. Rootkits**
- **Definition:** Malware providing root/administrator-level access (privilege escalation).
- **Placement:** User apps, OS, boot sectors, firmware.
- **Detection:** Host-based intrusion detection systems (HIDS) via file integrity/pattern analysis.

**E. Privilege Escalation**
- **Horizontal:** Lateral movement across systems with same privilege level.
- **Vertical:** Moving from general user to root/admin-level privileges.
- **Example:** Compromising a low-privilege account on one server to gain admin on another.

**F. Time-of-Check / Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) Attack**
- **Targets:** Race conditions (multiple processes accessing same resource).
- **Mechanism:**
    1. System checks conditions (e.g., sufficient balance).
    2. Attacker intercepts and modifies the resource/transaction before execution.
    3. System executes the altered action without re-checking.
- **Example:** Intercepting a fund transfer between own accounts and redirecting it to attacker’s account.

### 3. Key Takeaway
Understand each of these application attacks—specifically how they exploit trust (session hijack), bypass authentication (backdoors), escalate privileges (rootkits), or exploit race conditions (TOCTOU).

- Focus: **Source code level vulnerabilities** based on OWASP Top 10 (web application security risks, but applicable to software in general).

## 2. Risk #6 – Security Misconfiguration
**Cause:**
- Unpatched software
- Default accounts (passwords not reset)
- Lack of system hardening

**Consequence:** Increased attack surface → higher chance of compromise.

**Mitigation:**
- Follow industry best practices / regulations
- Disable anything not required (software, functionality, services)
- Regularly test and assess for compliance and best practices

---

## 3. Risk #7 – Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)
**Definition:** Unauthorized script/code injected into a webpage, executed in victim’s browser (browser-side injection attack). Exploits trust between browser and web server.

**Three types:**
- **Stored XSS** – Malicious script stored on target server → executed when user requests data.
- **Reflected XSS** – Malicious script comes from victim’s HTTP request (e.g., link with embedded script).
- **DOM-based XSS** – Modifies DOM environment to execute injected code (focuses on API/HTML/XML structure).

**Blind XSS:** Code stored and reflected, but attacker cannot see if successful.

**Mitigation:**
- Use modern scripting languages with **escape sequences** (e.g., Ruby, React JavaScript).
- Implement **Content Security Policy (CSP)** in HTML – permit by exception, deny by default.

---

## 4. Risk #8 – Insecure Deserialization
**Definitions:**
- **Serialization** – Converting object data format for communication/storage.
- **Deserialization** – Reversing the process to reuse the object.

**Common use:** JSON, also XML, Python, etc.

**Key concern:** Lack of control during conversion to/from objects.

**Mitigation:**
- Use **digital certificates / mutual authentication** for critical apps performing serialization.
- **Sandbox/isolate** deserialization code.
- **Restrict connectivity** to critical apps that perform serialization.
- Only execute API/connections with **trusted software**.

---

## 5. Risk #9 – Components with Known Vulnerabilities
**Cause:** Using components (libraries, OS, legacy apps/hardware) with known vulnerabilities.

**Consequence:** Increased risk of exploitation.

**Mitigation:**
- Identify known vulnerabilities (e.g., National Vulnerability Database, CVEs, vendor sites).
- Continuously monitor.
- Apply compensating controls.
- If critical/high risk → consider discontinuing use and migrating to newer applications.

---

## 6. Risk #10 – Insufficient Logging & Monitoring
**Consequence:** Prevents discovery of threats, vulnerabilities, and attacks.

**Mitigation:**
- Log all changes to:
  - Critical system services
  - Privilege levels
  - Accounts
  - Communications
- (Detailed coverage in separate logging/monitoring video.)

---

## 7. Takeaway for Exam
Understand each risk and its **mitigation** strategies.

- **Avoid hardcoded credentials** (passwords, tokens) → risk of exposure in production or public repos.
- **Restrict privileged escalation** (root/admin) unless absolutely necessary → reduces exploitation risk.

---

## 1. Definition
- **Software-defined security** = security functions included as part of developed software (code).
- Started with virtualizing security functions (e.g., firewalls, IDS/IPS, appliances).
- Now part of broader *software-defined everything*.

---

## 2. Related Software-Defined Concepts
- **Software-Defined Networking (SDN)** – virtualized network resources creating a single converged network.
- **Infrastructure as Code** – software-defined infrastructure, provisioning, automation, management.
- **Software-Defined Data Center** – virtualizes all infrastructure resources for data center operations (compute, network, storage).

---

## 3. Implementing Security as Code
- **Security as Code** = building security processes into DevOps or other development workflows.
- Typically part of **DevOps / CI/CD** → called **DevSecOps** (security built into the entire lifecycle).

---

## 4. Key Techniques
- **Configuration as Code** – standardize and apply approved configurations → create a **gold image** (hardened, compliant, immutable).
- **Policy as Code** – combines infrastructure as code + configuration as code + access controls/policies → ensures immutability.
- Changes require proper change control and configuration management.

---

## 5. Best Practices & Considerations
- Identify which security controls can be implemented as code (not all can, e.g., some administrative controls).
- Map current processes and infrastructure changes → find vulnerabilities → minimize them with code.
- Insert **gates** (security checks/tests) at vulnerable points in the pipeline.
- Gates do **not** slow the pipeline; they identify and report issues for human review.
- Accept risk only if within tolerance; otherwise, revisit the problem.
- Regularly test security-as-code products as part of SDLC/DevOps.
- Perform compliance assessments as part of continuous delivery.

---

## 6. Bottom Line
- Understand the purpose of software-defined security.
- Follow security-as-code best practices.
